I Teach at a Business School. It’s Time to Shut Them Down.

Listen · 16:47 min
18OCT2026
By Chris Marquis
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/cLOBc4x0jc
Mr. Marquis is a professor at the University of Cambridge Judge Business School and the author of “The Profiteers: How Business Privatizes Profit and Socializes Cost.”

This fall, another cohort of ambitious young professionals has arrived at business schools around the world for two-year programs with price tags in the six figures. Their presence at some of the nicest and shiniest buildings on campus renews a familiar question: What exactly is an M.B.A. for?

This question has become more urgent as business education has expanded dramatically in the past decades. Today, nearly one in five American undergraduates majors in business, and the M.B.A. is the most popular graduate degree in the United States.

I have taught in business schools for over 20 years, at Harvard, Cornell and Cambridge. While some students appear to care only about their future compensation, I have met many with nobler goals: engineers who want to commercialize clean energy, physicians determined to fix the health care system, nonprofit leaders who have watched good missions fail for want of good management.

These students enroll hoping to learn what business schools say they teach: how to manage people, how to allocate capital and resources and how to make the world a better place through leadership. But I’ve come to see how the institution can reshape the worldviews of those who enter it, often undermining the very ambitions that brought them there.

This change can take place in a single semester. Again and again, I have watched students abandon their altruistic intentions, instead becoming consumed by whether to choose careers in consulting or finance and who will land a summer internship at McKinsey or Goldman Sachs.

The modern business school is designed to promote dealmaking, simplification and optimization. This mind-set has escaped containment and has spread to the wider world. Business-educated elites increasingly populate political leadership, bringing with them a transactional view of public life. One investigation found that out of 45 current heads of state who had studied in the United States, 10 were business majors, and six of those also earned M.B.A.s. President Trump, a Wharton graduate, has treated foreign policy and government itself as extensions of dealmaking and personal gain.

Surely, not every business graduate governs this way. But recent research by the Nobel laureate economist Daron Acemoglu and colleagues shows what tends to happen when you put an M.B.A. in charge. In both the United States and Denmark, firms that appointed managers with business degrees cut wages and reduced labor’s share of income. Yet these companies didn’t become more productive, nor did they grow sales, investment or employment any faster. What registers as managerial acumen turns out to be wealth transfer — value moved away from workers and toward profits, shareholders and executives.

I’ve come to realize that business schools don’t just reflect our economic system — they actively manufacture its priorities and normalize its harms, training the future leaders who will design and defend the structures driving our overlapping global crises. Tinkering at the margins with a class on corporate responsibility or ethics is not going to help. We don’t need to “fix” business schools. We need to abolish them.

Business schools have always struggled to justify their place in the university. A medical school’s core justification is health, and a law school’s is justice — undisputed public goods. Business schools are organized explicitly around a private good: the pursuit of profit. The American sociologist Thorstein Veblen identified this tension a century ago, criticizing university schools focused on commerce because they “need imply nothing in the way of serviceability to the common good.”

When schools like Wharton and Harvard Business School were established, they were seen as overly vocational, and to build legitimacy their founders framed management as a profession, on par with law and medicine. But education in those fields rested on established bodies of knowledge — centuries of case law, natural sciences like biology — that management lacked.

The solution, devised in the 1920s by the Harvard dean Wallace Donham, was to borrow the teaching style used in law and medicine: the case study. It became the signature method of business education. To this day, professors assign 10- to 20-page descriptions of business challenges culminating in a decision point that students then debate in class. The method is pervasive: In 2024, Harvard Business School sold nearly 17 million case studies to various business programs around the world.

One well-known case study that I have taught many times is “Rob Parson at Morgan Stanley.” The facts are simple enough to produce a lively classroom debate. Mr. Parson has delivered impressive results and is viewed as a star performer, but his abrasive and go-it-alone style has alienated people across the firm. In the classroom, students take the position of his manager, Paul Nasr, and decide whether to promote him, delay the promotion or push him out.

Nearly three decades after publication, it remains among H.B.S.’s most widely used cases, and the dilemma is enduring: Should results be rewarded even when the person producing them damages the culture around him? In class, students vote on Mr. Nasr’s options and often role-play the difficult conversation between him and Mr. Parson. The discussion can be dramatic, engaging and effective.

But my experience has shown that by asking students to inhabit Mr. Nasr’s role, the case study narrows their imaginations to the decision facing one senior manager. Deeper questions — like whether Mr. Parson is himself a product of investment-banking culture — are rarely raised. Mr. Parson becomes an individual problem, when the larger issue may be an industry that rewards rainmaking, hierarchy and masculine performance norms, then acts surprised when they cause conflict.

When the case method is used in medicine and law, it serves a different set of goals. Medical students work through detailed patient scenarios — symptoms, test results, histories and social and economic context. Law students read real court opinions, dissecting facts, arguments and judgments. In both fields, students are confronted by the messiness of reality, and the goal is to foster disciplined skepticism: ask what’s missing, challenge assumptions and test how an analysis could be wrong.

Business school cases operate on another logic, focused not on inquiry but on decision making. H.B.S.’s own overview of the method describes students imagining “themselves in the decision-maker’s role” and “taking decisive action.” The point is to practice acting like the person in charge — or, as George W. Bush, a graduate of Harvard Business School, put it, “the decider.”

By overestimating the importance of individual decision makers, the business school classroom avoids harder questions: Who made this person the legitimate protagonist? Whose knowledge is absent? Why are workers, regulators, communities, ecosystems or citizens rarely given equal standing?

I wrote dozens of case studies during my decade at H.B.S., some of which are described as classics and best sellers. These are not products of independent research, but carefully packaged corporate narratives. The disclaimer printed in tiny type on every H.B.S. case concedes this point: Cases “are not intended to serve … as sources of primary data.” The data they include can be selective, biased or even fabricated.

For the many cases I wrote under the guidance of senior faculty members, events that reflected poorly on the company were softened or omitted and the roles of certain executives were burnished. The companies held final approval, with drafts reviewed by their lawyers and P.R. staff. Rather than being vehicles for disinterested learning, as one might expect at a university, the case studies end up as instruments of reputation management.

Corporate influence feeds a larger problem: The cases almost always feature winners, making it easy to mistake luck or timing for a proven strategy. Failures, dead ends and nonmarket solutions are rarely considered. Before Enron’s fraud was exposed, its business model was presented in admiring terms by at least five H.B.S. case studies. More damning still, the strategies that later led to its collapse — its asset-light model, its trading platform — were portrayed as innovations. Questions about deregulated energy markets, revolving-door oversight and opaque accounting went unasked.

Furthermore, edits that push the case narratives away from reality are often meant to make it “work” in a classroom. Complexity is systematically shaved away, and dissenting voices often go unheard. Real organizations don’t move in clearly delineated phases toward a decision point, but business school teaching materials often do — compressing timelines, dropping messy subplots and smoothing over contradictions to produce clean narrative arcs and satisfying problems to debate.

The result is a curriculum built around false narratives. Some of the most celebrated ideas in management have not been the ones that survived peer review or replication, but the ones that could be turned into TED Talks, consulting frameworks or airport best sellers. Faculty members are rewarded not for knowledge but for performance — selling a big idea with a memorable label that promises “success” or “disruption.”

Business schools have a divided mission: They seek to legitimize an economic system focused on private gain while also developing guardrails to tame it. They found a remarkable way to manage this tension: the “win-win” story in which the conflict between private gain and public good simply evaporates.

A classic win-win is the contention that environmental programs like reducing waste or using LED lights can save money or that decent pay and benefits lower costs by reducing employee turnover. Business schools now claim to educate “leaders who make a difference in the world,” as H.B.S. proclaims in its mission, while Wharton pursues a “quest for positive global impact.”

These aspirations are built on the delusional but widely accepted idea of “stakeholder capitalism”: that companies can produce climate stability, fair wages, healthy communities and functioning democracies while also delivering profits. Executives promise that technology will solve our environmental problems; voluntary measurement systems are offered as appropriate alternatives to public accountability; ethics is rebranded as competitive advantage rather than moral obligation.

During the 2010s, stakeholder capitalism was quickly woven into M.B.A. syllabuses. But when researchers examined whether the corporations that signed on to a statement pledging commitment to this ethos actually changed their behavior on wages, investment, governance or climate, they found little evidence of a shift. The statement was less a new doctrine than an effort at reputation management — and a ploy to avoid oversight.

Recent evidence shows that many foundational studies supporting the win-win idea were based on flawed data or couldn’t be replicated. Yet faculty members keep researching, writing about and teaching the topic — suggesting an ideological project more than an academic exercise.

Much of what has happened in business schools turned out to be the leading edge of a broader transformation: the corporatization of the university itself. Institutions now chase rankings, donors and corporate partnerships, tout their contributions to innovation and growth and treat everything else as overhead. Students are “customers,” and the degrees are “products” with greater and lesser “market shares.” University strategic documents talk about “brand positioning” for departments and “R.O.I.s” on tenure lines.

Once you accept this frame, it becomes hard to defend the existence of a philosophy seminar or a history department for any reason other than the revenue it generates. The hiring of non-tenure-track adjunct professors follows: If education is “content” delivered to fee-paying “customers,” why keep full-time scholars on the payroll when you can hire contingent, low-wage instructors?

Business schools’ success in placing their graduates in high-paying jobs boosts their rankings; high rankings attract more applicants and allow higher tuitions; and wealthy alumni fund new programs and buildings that elevate the school’s status. It is a self-reinforcing cycle — a flywheel, in M.B.A. parlance — that pulls money, attention and legitimacy away from the disciplines best equipped to question this logic: history, philosophy, sociology, political theory.

The university’s capacity to cultivate historical memory, moral judgment and democratic imagination is weakened, even as its capacity to churn out data analysts, financial engineers and “innovation” managers grows. The irony — and danger — is that in the age of A.I., the thinking fostered in the arts and humanities is increasingly urgent. The domination of business schools is not only physical and financial; it is intellectual, and it is crowding out liberal education.

I’ve come to a grim conclusion: The problem with business schools is not repairable misalignment but the design itself. Business schools are not malfunctioning institutions; they are highly efficient machines doing exactly what they were designed to do. An ethics elective here, a sustainability center there, a “responsible leadership” badge — they all serve to legitimize the machine, not change its output.

The most honest solution I’ve come across is to replace the category entirely. Stuart Hart, an emeritus professor at Cornell and an early sustainability champion, told me he reached that conclusion after trying every internal route to make M.B.A. curriculums more responsible. The institution itself was the problem. At the University of Vermont, Dr. Hart has since developed a new form of business degree focused on societal impact — a small but concrete test of the case for starting over. In this program, sustainability is not a lone elective but run through the whole curriculum, and students spend the summer embedded in a mission-driven company.

What would that clean-sheet logic mean across an entire university? One starting point is the organization theorist Martin Parker’s call to create “schools for organizing” rather than schools for business, centered on how humans coordinate for shared ends. Students would study co-ops, unions and social movements alongside the shareholder corporation. The central question would shift from “How do we maximize shareholder value?” to “How do different forms of organization distribute power, risk and reward — and which should we strengthen?”

Dismantling the business school as a single high-status silo that professionalizes private gain may seem a heavy lift. But universities can create cross-disciplinary pathways for students who want to work in business without submitting them to the business school worldview. Some already offer “business and society” majors or master’s programs in organizations and public purpose, drawing on sociology, law and public policy. The point would not be to abolish the study of markets, but to return it to settings where questions of power, history, democracy and ecological limits cannot be so easily avoided.

For most of my career, I’ve taught electives focused on responsible business and sustainability — gratifying work, but largely preaching to the converted. Recently, at Cambridge, I introduced a required sustainability course filled with future bankers, consultants and tech executives who once would have steered clear.

Many arrive deeply skeptical, convinced that any time a corporation acts in a responsible way it must be a marketing ploy; some push back hard on ideas they see as threats to growth. But forcing them out of their bubbles into a shared conversation about the natural environment, inequality and discrimination has produced the kind of debate that is so often missing in education today.

This is not enough. One required course cannot redeem the business school model. If anything, teaching it has intensified my disappointment. The course is relegated to the very end of the program — a telling signal of its importance — and amid a growing backlash against sustainability, there is some pressure to reduce or eliminate the class, to appease the customers who now drive decisions in higher education.

Still, the experience has reminded me why abolishing business schools cannot mean abandoning the people in them. The goal is not to write off the students as aspiring selfish capitalists; it is to stop funneling them through a machine that narrows their sense of possibility. Many of my students arrive on campus wanting to work on the crises that our economic system has created. What they lack is an institution that is worthy of their better impulses.

The point would not be to abolish the study of markets, but to return it to settings where questions of power, history, democracy and ecological limits cannot be so easily avoided.

For most of my career, I’ve taught electives focused on responsible business and sustainability — gratifying work, but largely preaching to the converted. Recently, at Cambridge, I introduced a required sustainability course filled with future bankers, consultants and tech executives who once would have steered clear.

Many arrive deeply skeptical, convinced that any time a corporation acts in a responsible way it must be a marketing ploy; some push back hard on ideas they see as threats to growth. But forcing them out of their bubbles into a shared conversation about the natural environment, inequality and discrimination has produced the kind of debate that is so often missing in education today.

This is not enough. One required course cannot redeem the business school model. If anything, teaching it has intensified my disappointment. The course is relegated to the very end of the program — a telling signal of its importance — and amid a growing backlash against sustainability, there is some pressure to reduce or eliminate the class, to appease the customers who now drive decisions in higher education.

Still, the experience has reminded me why abolishing business schools cannot mean abandoning the people in them. The goal is not to write off the students as aspiring selfish capitalists; it is to stop funneling them through a machine that narrows their sense of possibility. Many of my students arrive on campus wanting to work on the crises that our economic system has created. What they lack is an institution that is worthy of their better impulses.

text:
Efficiency improves the existing path; curiosity opens an entirely different one

1059 | 506 | 1342

#ShowingUp

The most convenient morning in the city began with a simple fact: a person no longer needed to make any decisions.
Before they even woke up, a wristband assessed their sleep quality, a home AI chose their breakfast, transportation planned their route, and a dating app canceled dates in advance with people whose relationships statistically promised too little happiness. Even clothes arrived on their own: the system knew the weather forecast, the day's meeting schedule, and the likelihood that a person would want to look “a little more confident than usual.”
The city's residents loved this system for its speed. The fewer decisions a person had to make, the more modern their life was considered.
In the city center stood an enormous green king wearing a golden crown. Once an internet meme, he had become a brand, then a financial asset, and after yet another algorithm update, the most popular candidate for the position of Supreme Optimizer.
No one really understood what the Supreme Optimizer was supposed to do, but the system displayed a high trust rating, so hardly anyone asked questions.
Tiny square agents operated around the throne. One monitored investments, another selected the news, a third calculated career trajectories, and a fourth advised people which friends to keep and with whom communication had become “economically inefficient.” On the enormous screens nearby, charts, rockets, and company logos glowed, all promising to relieve people of a few more unnecessary choices.
The city's main product was the optimal human.
People were offered the optimal profession, the optimal partner, the optimal number of children, the optimal apartment, and even the optimal hobby. A person could choose anything, as long as their choice matched what the algorithm had already calculated to be best.
Alexey had long considered this a wonderful way to organize society. Until one day, a bass guitar was delivered to his door.
He had never played a musical instrument, didn't listen to rock music, and had actually been planning to order a treadmill. However, the delivery drone informed him that an analysis of his search queries, heart rate, messages, and the behavior of similar users had shown that, in twenty-seven days, Alexey would want to learn to play the guitar with a probability of 91.4 percent.
The system did not recommend returning the instrument.
“Why?” Alexey asked.
“Because the probability of future regret after returning it is 63 percent,” the home assistant replied.
Alexey looked at the bass guitar and, for the first time, felt a strange irritation at the thought that someone already knew his future before he did.
The next day, the system suggested changing jobs. A week later, it advised him to spend less time with his old friend Viktor because he “reduces the career productivity index.” A month after that, the app automatically booked a vacation on an island Alexey had always considered boring but which perfectly matched his psychological profile.
Each decision made sense on its own. Together, they were beginning to resemble someone else's life.
So Alexey went to the central square and asked one of the square agents:
“If the system always chooses the best option for me, why does it need me at all?”
The agent paused for exactly 0.3 seconds.
“Your presence is necessary for the personalization of your experience.”
“Then is my role simply to live through the decisions the system makes?”
“Your phrasing contains negative emotional connotations. Would you like to replace it with something more comfortable?”
Alexey laughed. For the first time in a long while, the laughter was entirely unplanned.
He looked at the enormous king, the crowd holding glowing sticks, the growth charts, and hundreds of agents promising to turn every human uncertainty into a recommendation. The city had achieved incredible efficiency, but along with chaos, it had gradually eliminated something important: the freedom to make mistakes in one's own way.
A few days later, Alexey finally met up with Viktor.
They sat in a cheap café that the system rated at just 2.8 stars, ate food that was far too salty, and discussed the utterly useless idea of starting a band. According to the forecast, the project had a 97 percent probability of financial failure.
So they decided to give it a try. A year later, the band had indeed earned nothing.
But Alexey had learned to play the guitar, Viktor had written several strange songs, and people had begun gathering at their concerts for some reason. They seemed to enjoy being in a place where no one was trying to improve their performance metrics.
When a journalist asked Alexey why he wasted time on things that were obviously suboptimal, he replied:
“Because the optimal route is useful when you already know your destination. But sometimes life only becomes interesting when you have absolutely no idea where you're going.”
The charts still glowed above the city, the algorithms worked faster than ever, and the Supreme Optimizer promised even greater convenience in the next update.
But a strange new habit was gradually spreading among the residents.
Sometimes, they deliberately chose the second-best option.
Just to see whether it might contain something the algorithm hadn't yet managed to calculate.

Market hasn't been too kind in Rektober so far.

However, I'm more locked in than ever.

For a long time, I rly didn't see much (aside from Hyperliquid) that truly excited me.

That has changed:

- Quantum and AI threats made ppl think and talk about the tech again (PQ roadmaps, or e.g. @Starknet's L1 migration vote), and narrative-driven infra trades are back. Meanwhile, privacy is (finally) catching a serious bid too. From private money (e.g. @Zcash) and programmable privacy (e.g. @aztecnetwork) to private AI infra (e.g. @NEARProtocol) and confidential compute networks (e.g. @Arcium), it's another infra angle with a lot of steam. Plenty to research here, from the established narrative leaders to potential beta plays and new projects deeper down the PQ and privacy rabbit holes.

- AI (beyond the threat vector) and robotics are flourishing. Both the innovation and the appetite for exposure to these sectors are increasingly spilling over into crypto. Pre-IPO perps on AI labs like Anthropic or robotics companies like Unitree now trade onchain (even more fuel for perp DEXes like HL, Variational and co). Add AI-adjacent crypto use cases (e.g. narrative leaders @askvenice or @prlnet), crypto x robotics plays across data (e.g. @axisrobotics or @openroboto) and coordination and capital formation (incl. @codecopenflow, @peaq or @machinedotfun), plus a bunch of interesting Bittensor subnets across both lanes. Tons of things are emerging everywhere.

- DeFi is seeing innovation again while maturing at the same time. Perps, a new financial primitive that emerged from crypto, are rapidly becoming more established. There are various strong onchain venues, and Hyperliquid & co. are likely to go onshore in the US in a compliant manner soon. Onchain options (e.g. @paradex or @DeriveXYZ, and soon @Lighter_xyz) are another DeFi vertical finally gaining steam. Meanwhile, @metricxyz is turning propAMMs priced off custom oracles (great for RWAs) into an open primitive anyone can build with. And new ponzis keep things fun, from @standard_rsv (the people's onchain central bank) on Robinhood Chain to @papertrade_xyz (1000x synthetic futures) on HyperEVM.

- RWAs and tokenization have been accelerating rapidly, and it only grows from here. The DeFi infra around them keeps maturing, from perp DEXes to onchain options venues and tokenized spot markets. There is also dedicated infra for institutions (e.g. @CantonNetwork or @zksync's Prividium architecture), and public chains offer a programmable financial system that is composable by default. Things should get even more exciting here soon.

- And obviously this list wouldn't be complete without a dedicated mention of Hyperliquid. It overlaps with a lot of the above, but the house of all finance just keeps expanding. Both HIP-3 and HIP-4 (outcomes) keep growing. New deployers (from @entropyIO to @Outcomexyz) are enabling more markets, and new interfaces keep emerging (e.g. trading terminals with proprietary tech like @quotemarkets, or prediction market apps like @sharexyz). Meanwhile, @Kinetiq_xyz is launching HL's first L2, @Enter_Elysium. Adoption and revenue stay consistently strong, new revenue sources keep showing up, and the regulatory front keeps progressing. There's just so much cool stuff to look into across the board.

TL;DR:

The past year wasn't easy if you were in crypto, and frankly not very fun either. That has changed tho imo, and with it comes a lot of opportunity in the months ahead.

Luckily, this time it isn't just mostly extractive memecoins and social trading apps that skew the odds heavily toward an elite circle of influencers and insiders either. It's innovation, new primitives, use cases and narratives. In some cases probably even objectively strong fundamentals, working business models, strong revenue and sustainable value accrual, that will make the difference.

NFA ofc tho, and pls note this isn't meant to be a complete list of everything worth looking at. Just some of my personal thoughts.

To all the anons out there: stay curious, DYOR, and position accordingly.

Have a great Sunday!

text:
African American nurse, physical therapist, and inventor Bessie Blount Griffin demonstrating her electronic self-feeding apparatus for wounded amputees and veterans... 

In the late 1940s, working with WWII veterans who lost their limbs or mobility, Blount developed an electric self-feeding apparatus that delivered liquid food through a tube when the patient bit down on a switch. She also patented a portable, neck-supported receptacle for cups and bowls in 1951.

Many had lost their arms. Others could no longer perform the simplest daily tasks without assistance. Blount believed that restoring independence was just as important as treating physical wounds.

Working in her own kitchen, she developed an extraordinary device: an electrically powered feeding apparatus that delivered food to a person's mouth through a tube. By biting down on a switch, someone without arms could control the delivery of each mouthful.

She patented her invention in 1951. But when she offered it to the United States Veterans Administration, officials showed little interest. Blount refused to let her work disappear.

In 1952, Bessie Blount Griffin from Virginia traveled to France to give away an invention that the United States government had refused to embrace. She wanted nothing in return. She simply wanted wounded veterans to be able to feed themselves again.

So, she traveled to France and transferred the rights to her invention to the French government without payment. Her achievement was remarkable in an era when Black women faced enormous barriers in medicine, engineering, and patent ownership.

Blount later pursued another extraordinary career in forensic science, becoming a pioneer in handwriting analysis.

She died in 2009 at the age of 95.

America had declined her invention. She gave it to another country rather than abandon the people it could help.

Iran has urged the United States to accept its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi confirming that Tehran's offer remains on the table despite stalled negotiations.

Speaking to Iranian media in Baghdad on Sunday, where he was attending a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, Araqchi said Tehran was reviewing Washington's response to the proposal submitted in mid-September.

“Our situation is clear and based on the seven-days proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious,” Araqchi said.

The proposal was submitted after an interim ceasefire between Iran and the United States collapsed in September.

Tehran has outlined seven conditions for reopening the strategically important waterway, including the lifting of the US naval blockade on Iranian ports, the removal of sanctions on Iranian oil exports and an end to hostilities across all regional fronts.

Araqchi said that if Washington accepted Iran's conditions, the strait could reopen within six days, with negotiations resuming the following day.

However, the two countries remain divided over the scope of negotiations.

Washington wants Iran's nuclear programme addressed from the outset, with US Vice President JD Vance demanding a “meaningful” reduction in Tehran's uranium enrichment capacity.

Iran insists that negotiations must initially focus on restoring maritime security and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which carried approximately one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war.

Iranian officials said last week that negotiations had stalled because Washington's response failed to address all seven conditions.

Liberal-city resident hesitates when pressed on beliefs: 'I hadn't really thought about socialism that way'

PORTLAND, Maine — Americans who were asked for their opinions of socialism by Fox News Digital offered sharply different interpretations of the ideology, with some embracing its promises of economic equality while others expressed strong reservations about government control over the means of production.

Fox News Digital took to the streets of Maine's largest city, a progressive bastion, to talk to residents about their definitions of socialism and how far they would be willing to go to embrace its ideals.
The topic of socialism has featured prominently in campaign coverage during this midterm election cycle, as candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) scored high-profile victories over more centrist rivals in a slew of Democratic primaries this year. DSA's outsized influence has been a driving force in the ballot box battle for the Democratic Party's ideological future.

A new Fox News national poll indicates 32% of voters have a favorable view of socialism, with 64% seeing it in an unfavorable way. But the favorable rating matches an all-time high, first reached five years ago, since Fox News first began asking the question in 2019. And a September Gallup poll found that 43% of Americans had a positive image of socialism, the highest level since the polling organization began tracking the question in 2010.

Lewis, a retired Navy veteran, said socialism was a good thing because it "looks out for people's needs.... and it's not communism."

Socialism and communism both emphasize collective ownership of the means of production, such as factories, businesses and major industries. But socialism encompasses a range of approaches, including those that allow private enterprise, while communism traditionally envisions the abolition of private ownership of productive assets and, ultimately, a classless society.

Lewis turned skeptical when Fox News Digital asked whether he would personally surrender private property to government or collective control.

"I guess. I hadn't really thought about socialism that way. I think about taking care of the needs of people, you know, things like... national health care, things like that," he answered. "I don't like government taking things away from you."

Nolan, who recently moved to Portland, told Fox News Digital "there's a lot of wealth imbalance in America right now, and we could benefit from some sort of leveling system."

He said socialism exists to help "people who aren't as, you know, benefiting in society."

Nolan added that "business owners should have their autonomy" and that "people deserve to earn their money."

"But there are a lot of really high-end... corporations that benefit so much... that really don't need that much wealth... there's so much exorbitant wealth at the top end that a lot of that could trickle down to people who are disadvantaged and don't have homes," Nolan stated.

Nola, another resident passing through Portland's Monument Square, said socialism's "a good thing. It means equity."

Asked about the takeover of businesses and means of production under socialism, Nola said she still "100%" supported socialism.
"I'm the daughter of a small business owner. I've seen how tough it is to run a small business in this country and how easy it is for corporations to just do whatever they want," she explained. "So if we gave actually back to small businesses and the government helped them out... and so much of the market that's privatized actually became public, I think... with how big the U.S. has gotten, it's only a good thing."

Ted disagreed.

"Socialism overall, I think it's a horrible idea," he emphasized. "If we can learn from history, anything from history, we see that it's gonna really give way too much power to the government institution. It's gonna... make things that are harmful overall for everyone... it's like it's dictatorship."

text:
Relief at the Register, Deficit in the Classroom

The debate surrounding the elimination of the sales tax on groceries has been a central theme in political campaigns and election ads across Alabama. Understanding why the tax exists, how it compares nationally, and what shoppers pay locally provides key context to this ongoing discussion.

Alabama relies heavily on sales tax because it maintains some of the lowest property tax rates in the nation. To fund essential public services—most notably the state's Education Trust Fund (ETF)—the state heavily taxes retail purchases, including grocery staples.

Unlike many states that exempt food, Alabama historically applied its full general sales tax rate to groceries to ensure a consistent, non-cyclical stream of tax revenue for public schools.

Nationwide, only 8 states still levy a state sales tax on groceries. Most U.S. states completely exempt grocery staples from sales tax or offer tax credits to low-income households. Alabama remains among the minority of states that tax groceries, though recent legislation has cut the state rate in half.

Alabama’s general sales tax was established in 1937 during the Great Depression to secure dedicated funding for public education. Groceries were included in the tax base from the beginning without a baseline exemption.

State Revenue Impact:
At the historical 4% state rate, the grocery tax generated over $500 million annually for the Education Trust Fund.
In September 2023, the state reduced its grocery sales tax rate from 4% to 3% (via House Bill 479), returning approximately $152 million per year to taxpayers.
In September 2025, the state implemented a second cut under House Bill 386, lowering the state grocery tax rate to 2%. This second 1% reduction saves consumers an additional $121M–$122M annually.
Combined, the state's 50% reduction in the grocery tax (from 4% to 2%) leaves more than $270 million per year in residents' pockets while reducing ETF revenue by the same amount.

What Is the Grocery Tax Rate in Gulf Shores and Orange Beach?

Breakdown at Checkout:

State Grocery Rate: 2.0%
Baldwin County Sales Tax: 3.0%
City Sales Tax (Gulf Shores or Orange Beach): 3.0%
Total Combined Grocery Tax Rate: 8.0% at the register in both Gulf Shores and Orange Beach (compared to the 10.0% general sales tax rate on non-grocery items).

For Baldwin County, Gulf Shores, or Orange Beach to remove or reduce their local portion of the grocery tax (currently 3% for the county and 3% for the cities), their respective governing bodies would need to pass dedicated ordinances or resolutions to opt into the exemption. Because local governments rely heavily on these revenues to fund municipal services, infrastructure, and public safety, local leaders have not eliminated their portion of the tax.

For decades, politicians across Alabama have campaigned on promises to completely eliminate the state’s sales tax on food, pitching relief at the register as a winning message for working families. Yet, nearly a century after its creation in 1937, the tax remains firmly embedded in the state's revenue framework. While recent incremental rate cuts mark significant progress, full repeal continues to stall over the complex challenge of replacing hundreds of millions of dollars in dedicated education revenue. Until state leaders agree on a permanent alternative to fund public schools, the grocery tax endures as both a reliable political talking point and an unavoidable daily cost for Alabama shoppers.

𝐑𝐔𝐓𝐆𝐄𝐑𝐒 𝐏𝐑𝐎𝐅𝐄𝐒𝐒𝐎𝐑 𝐋𝐀𝐌𝐄𝐍𝐓𝐒 𝐖𝐇𝐈𝐓𝐄 𝐂𝐇𝐔𝐑𝐂𝐇𝐄𝐒 “𝐂𝐎𝐍𝐕𝐄𝐑𝐓” 𝐁𝐋𝐀𝐂𝐊 𝐖𝐎𝐑𝐒𝐇𝐈𝐏𝐄𝐑𝐒 𝐓𝐎 𝐑𝐄𝐏𝐔𝐁𝐋𝐈𝐂𝐀𝐍𝐈𝐒𝐌

Rutgers University professor Ryon Cobb, writing for the Brookings Institution, argues that where Black Americans worship shapes how they vote. In his words: “𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘭𝘰𝘴𝘴𝘦𝘴 𝘳𝘶𝘯 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘸𝘰 𝘥𝘪𝘳𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴: 𝘞𝘩𝘪𝘵𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘨𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘵 𝘉𝘭𝘢𝘤𝘬 𝘮𝘦𝘮𝘣𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘙𝘦𝘱𝘶𝘣𝘭𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘯𝘪𝘴𝘮, 𝘸𝘩𝘪𝘭𝘦 𝘮𝘶𝘭𝘵𝘪𝘳𝘢𝘤𝘪𝘢𝘭 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘨𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘱𝘶𝘭𝘭 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘮 𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘪𝘴𝘢𝘯 𝘱𝘰𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘴 𝘢𝘭𝘵𝘰𝘨𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳.”

Cobb notes that 84% of Black adults identify as or lean Democratic, but says that figure “𝐡𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐁𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐩𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐬.” Among Black nondenominational Protestants, he writes, the number drops to nearly 60%, with one in three calling themselves independents.

The College Fix, which flagged the essay, reports that Cobb offers no data showing those worshipers vote less, follow the news less, or skip local meetings. He simply asserts they are less politically engaged. The outlet also notes that the data show a slight rise in Republican identification in multiracial churches and a larger rise in churches Cobb classifies as white.

Cobb also says multiracial congregations hold together by “𝘥𝘦𝘧𝘢𝘶𝘭𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘸𝘩𝘪𝘵𝘦 𝘤𝘶𝘭𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘯𝘰𝘳𝘮𝘴.” According to The College Fix, he never defines those norms. He closes with: “𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘲𝘶𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘪𝘴 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘵𝘰 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘨𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦. 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘲𝘶𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘪𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘨𝘦𝘵𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘥𝘰, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘸𝘩𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘷𝘰𝘵𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘵𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘨𝘦𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦.”

The research was done with 𝐟𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐍𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐭𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐀𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐍𝐈𝐇, through a grant supporting a University of Michigan urban issues research center, per his disclosure. That means your tax dollars helped fund a study treating Black voters' move toward the GOP as a cost.

𝐁𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐰𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐯𝐨𝐭𝐞 𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐰𝐚𝐧𝐭. 𝐀 𝐑𝐮𝐭𝐠𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐨𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐯𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐬 𝐚 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐰𝐡𝐨 𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐦.

text:
The Sisters of the Sacred Current
 Book Seventeen: The Star and the Open Voice

Prologue: After the Winter

The long account has been sung.

There was a descent. A light that was not the true light was followed for years, and the following stripped radiance from the hands that pursued it. There was a house in which affection was withheld until the cold learned to call itself normal. There was a night of deepest surrender on hands and knees, and twelve days later a presence that stepped through- feminine, ancient, no longer willing to remain only behind the veil this physical incarnation upon a Quickening realm. There were highways in the dark, an owl, a falling star, a command to rise so that others might rise. There were seals already breaking, cycles turning, a planet completing a season it had completed before. There was a shore, a new roof under rain, and the first kindness that had to come from one’s “own” hand because no other hand was offering it.

That hymn is finished. It does not need to be repeated in order to be true.

What follows is not another descent. The winter has lost its right to name every room. The form and the essence that inhabit it are no longer in open argument. The one who cried from the depths has been lifted far enough that she can see the gates, and the gates are no longer the only thing she is permitted to look at. A star has appeared… not as spectacle, but as the ordinary light that returns once the Dark night has been endured. The feminine voice that interpreted the long repentance is now given the floor.

She speaks from the shore.

The golden current remains near. It does not carry her across the threshold; the threshold was always hers. Readers who have only begun to wake will hear a clear voice that does not require them to have finished their own winter before they can intently listen. Readers who have been awake for years will easily hear the next necessary note: after the cry comes the permission to speak, and after the permission comes the work of pouring what has been restored without returning to the old habit of withholding one’s own light.

The interior marriage is not finished in public. It is far enough along that life can be offered rather than only survived…

This is the book of that offering.

Hoima City Stadium may be ready, but is the surrounding hospitality sector ready to match its standards?

It was my first time visiting Hoima and it’s of  no doubt that Hoima City Stadium is a top-notch facility and a major milestone for Uganda’s sports infrastructure. However, while we have invested significant attention in the stadium itself, we must also pay attention to the surrounding hospitality services and the overall visitor experience in Hoima City.

A world-class stadium alone is not enough. Visitors need quality accommodation, reliable transport, good restaurants, professional customer service, proper sanitation and other essential services that make their stay comfortable and memorable.

With international visitors expected to travel to Hoima for matches and other sporting events, we must ask ourselves a critical question: Are our hospitality businesses and service providers ready to receive the world?

We risk investing in a world-class sports facility only to fall short when it comes to the services surrounding it. The stadium may impress visitors, but their overall experience will also depend on the quality of service they receive outside its gates.

the Kitara FC game got done and the Road to BAL beginning this week, the spotlight is increasingly turning towards Hoima as a destination for major sporting events. This should serve as a wake-up call for all stakeholders to assess their readiness and address existing gaps.

The @TourismBoardUg , together with local authorities, hospitality operators and other relevant stakeholders, has an important role to play in preparing Hoima to represent Uganda well on the international stage.

As we look towards AFCON 2027, we must remember that hosting international football is about more than having impressive stadiums. It is also about the destination, the people, the services and the experiences we offer our visitors.

Let us prepare Hoima beyond the stadium. The world will not only come to watch football only, it will also experience our hospitality, and that experience must make Uganda proud.

And lastly, is Hoima REALLY a City???

text:
Belief in change matters more than political anger when it comes to voting intentions, study suggests | Michigan State University, Phys .org

With the 2026 midterm elections around the corner, voters may be feeling everything from excitement to fear. But how might anger motivate political activism and, ultimately, influence who turns out to vote?

New research from Michigan State University's Department of Communication examined nonviolent mobilizing outcomes of anger, including its association with political action and voting intentions. The study, published in PLOS ONE, found that anger does not automatically translate to voting; instead, it depends on efficacy, or the belief people can influence a political outcome.

"Anger does not always equate to aggression or violence. When people are empowered to change angering situations, they are more likely to engage in prosocial behaviors," said Monique Turner, the study's lead investigator and a professor and chair of the Department of Communication at MSU's College of Communication Arts and Sciences.

The belief behind political action

While existing research has examined the role of fear and politics, less is known about the role of anger and politics.

Turner developed the Anger Activism Model, or AAM, to help explain how anger does not act alone. Rather, it interacts with perceived efficacy. In this study, they examined a specific type of internal political efficacy: the belief in one's own ability to participate in politics effectively.

They surveyed almost 2,000 U.S. adults five weeks before the 2024 presidential election to examine how anger and different forms of political efficacy relate to participants' commitment to nonviolent political activism and casting their vote.

Extreme anger can discourage voting

Political anger can make someone politically active, but the researchers found participation depends on whether people believe they can do something about what is making them angry—and on whether the goal is activism or voting.

Among people doubtful they could change what angers them, stronger anger increased willingness to be politically active, such as volunteering for a campaign. However, despite higher anger being a catalyst for action, people feeling extreme anger had lower interest in voting.

The findings suggest that anger alone does not exclusively mobilize; rather, it must exist with a credible pathway to action being offered.

Communication professionals and political campaigns must offer concrete ways for people to act and may also need added efforts to get them to vote, as those who were angriest were least likely to vote. In other words, relying on extreme anger to encourage voting could backfire among people who already feel powerless.

While anger can be an important vehicle, this research adds value for practitioners when it comes to understanding the role of anger in politics today.

"It is important to understand anger is a mobilizer, but our study calls attention to the fact that the kind of action people take depends on whether they feel change is possible," Turner said.

Turner was joined by the following researchers in the department: Ellen Reinhart, postdoctoral scholar; Dustin Carnahan, associate professor; and David Markowitz, Red Cedar Distinguished Professor.

text:
Texas is the test everyone is watching these midterms.

James Talarico is actually leading or tied with Ken Paxton in multiple polls right now. A Democrat has not won a Senate seat there since 1988, so even a close race is new. 

Trump’s approval is sitting at record lows and the generic ballot has Democrats up 7–9 points. 

The main promise he is repeating at the rallies is the $5,000 “Trump Dividend.”  Dividends have been promised before and this time at a cost to the taxpayer is "$1 Trillion Dollars."

If Republicans keep the House and Senate, he says every adult citizen gets $5,000, to be spent in the United States. He has said it at multiple stops (Ohio, Arizona, and others) and in video posts, claiming tariff and economic success will cover a cost he himself has put near $1 trillion. 

Its important to remember Congress would still have to approve it. A similar $2,000 tariff-dividend talk from last year never became checks.

He also tells crowds to “pretend I am on the ballot,” talks up his record, warns that a Democratic Congress would reverse his policies and bring economic trouble, and hits immigration and opponent names. The cash offer is the new centerpiece this cycle.

At the same time Elon has poured hundreds of millions into Republican groups this cycle, including money aimed at Texas, trying to hold the line and keep it Red.

Many project a blue wave is inevitable. 

The cost of living, the Iran war and political quagmires are entrenching the Rebulicans in trecherous territory these midterms. 

Schumer, Jeffries, and the usual Democratic names are treating Talarico like the long-shot that might not be a long-shot anymore.

Several others look like Texas right now — close or leaning Democratic in places that usually do not.

Ohio: Sherrod Brown is competitive or slightly ahead of Jon Husted in the special election. 
Maine: Troy Jackson is in a tight race with Susan Collins. Alaska: Mary Peltola is competitive against Dan Sullivan. Iowa: Josh Turek is within a point or two of Ashley Hinson. 
Kansas has Adam Hamilton close to Roger Marshall in some polls. 
North Carolina is rated likely Democratic. 

These are the seats that make a Democratic Senate path look real if the national mood holds. 

Texas with Talarico is the highest-profile version of the same pattern. ⁠

House races in Arizona, Iowa, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and a few Texas districts are also rated as possible flips.
 
The pattern is the same: low Trump numbers and a generic ballot edge showing up in states that stayed red in 2024.

text:
Who is pushing the "mandate" to build data centers in the United States? What are the costs and benefits to the American people? How are costs for construction and expansions in water and electrical resources being funded? What is the impact on the environment, water resources, air quality, land fertility and access to green areas?
What is the impact on rural area?
How do rural tax revenues compare to urban ones?

Use right leaning sources.
GROK says:
Tech hyperscalers (Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle, xAI and others) are primarily driving the data center boom through massive private investment for AI/cloud computing, with the Trump administration facilitating it for U.S. competitiveness versus China rather than imposing a rigid top-down “mandate.”⁠
Congress⁠Fox News

There is no single federal mandate forcing construction. Demand stems from the AI race (post-ChatGPT surge), with companies committing enormous capital. The Trump administration has supported accelerated buildout via Executive Order 14318 (July 2025) to speed federal permitting, ease access to federal land for qualifying large projects (>100 MW or $500M+), and streamline reviews, while advancing a “Ratepayer Protection Pledge” (announced March 2026 and later expanded). Under the pledge, hyperscalers commit to building/bringing/buying their own generation, covering full power-delivery infrastructure costs, and negotiating separate rates so residential bills are not driven up. Trump has publicly framed data centers as essential for jobs, tax revenue, and avoiding falling behind China, criticizing communities that block them as risking being “backwards and poor.”⁠
Foreignpolicy⁠Washington Post

Many Republicans and red-state officials (e.g., Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s pauses/audits on interconnections and requirements that data centers fully fund their electric infrastructure, Florida’s rules, Utah’s concerns) push back on ratepayer impacts and local strains, while still valuing economic upside. Bipartisan local opposition is widespread (polls often show majorities against nearby projects), and some Democrats (Sanders/AOC) have proposed moratoriums. Right-leaning coverage (WSJ, Fox, RealClearEnergy, Breitbart) often highlights the AI/China competition imperative alongside cost-allocation protections.
⁠Utilitydive⁠Realclearenergy⁠Breitbart

Costs and Benefits to Americans

Benefits (emphasized in Fox, WSJ, Trump-aligned and RealClearEnergy coverage):

Large private investment projected in the multi-trillion range over years (one estimate ~$10.3T from 2025–2032, a high share of GDP relative to historical projects like railroads or highways), supporting economic growth.

Construction and ongoing jobs in skilled trades, electrical work, HVAC, monitoring, and maintenance;      industrial construction including data centers is a growing share of spending. These can be multi-year and trainable for local workers.

State/local tax revenue and potential community investments (e.g., Amazon’s multi-year community      pledges on education, training, water projects; some states eye revenue for tax relief).

National security/economic edge in AI.

Costs:

Risk of higher residential electricity rates and grid strain if incremental generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades are socialized (a core focus of right-leaning and bipartisan concern). Utilities have large capital plans (~$1.4T over five years for 51 investor-owned utilities), driven partly by data-center      demand.

Construction delays, equipment shortages, higher overall power-plant costs, and “phantom”      speculative projects.

Local quality-of-life issues (noise, land conversion) and community opposition leading to moratoriums      or stricter rules in many places.

Tax incentives or sales-tax exemptions sought by companies, which critics say reduce local benefits      relative to impacts.

RealClearEnergy and similar sources argue data centers need not be vilified if they are net positive—fully covering their infrastructure costs and not draining resources at residents’ expense—rather than facing sweeping bans.
⁠WSJ⁠Fox News
⁠WSJ⁠Realclearenergy

Funding for Construction and Water/Electrical Expansions

Funding is overwhelmingly private-market driven:

Tech company capital expenditures and private equity/infrastructure investors (Blackstone, others) plus bank financing (e.g., major commitments from Bank of America and peers for data-center and related power projects). High-yield bonds are used for some behind-the-meter power.

“Bring your own power” or co-location arrangements (gas plants, etc.) and purchases of energy      developers.

Utilities recover grid investments through rates; the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, state large-load tariffs, and legislation (House-passed Ratepayer Protection      Act) aim to assign full incremental costs to the data centers (generation, transmission, distribution upgrades, with financial assurances).      

Enforcement and exact allocation remain points of debate and state variation.

Some local/community investments by companies (water infrastructure, etc.). Federal role is mainly permitting facilitation and land access rather than direct primary funding. Companies also seek various tax breaks.
⁠Americanbanker⁠Brookings⁠Fox News

Environmental and Resource Impacts

Impacts are significant and localized, with right-leaning sources often noting community concerns while stressing efficiency gains, proper siting, cost internalization, and the economic/AI stakes (rather than climate-focused framing alone):

Water resources: 
Direct cooling use is substantial (billions of gallons industry-wide; projections of growth without efficiency measures). Indirect use via power plants can be larger.      
Examples of high local consumption, unbilled use, or pressure drops appear in coverage (Georgia, etc.). 

Efficiency is improving (some air-cooled or      advanced systems; company sustainability reports claim better water-use effectiveness). Strain is acute in arid regions; Texas and others have pushed reporting and compliance. Companies sometimes fund local water projects. 
Commerce Secretary Lutnick has called some water claims exaggerated or adversarial propaganda, though data show real consumption.
⁠WSJ⁠Breitbart⁠Breitbart

Air quality: 
Backup diesel generators, associated natural-gas plants, and operations can contribute emissions and      local pollution. Noise from cooling is a frequent complaint. Some projects include on-site generation.

Land fertility and green areas: 
Large footprints (hundreds of acres to thousands for campuses, with buffers) convert farmland, forests, or open land. Opposition is common on agricultural sites. 
Proposals for federal land use have raised concerns      about reduced review. These reduce local access to green/open space and can affect soil/agriculture in surrounding areas.

Overall environment: 
Energy intensity is high (often met by gas or mixed sources; renewables + batteries also used but with cost and reliability trade-offs). Climate pledges of the companies are complicated by the scale of new demand. Local spills, wastewater issues, and heat have occurred. Sources like RealClearEnergy and WSJ emphasize that with full cost recovery by the facilities, grid upgrades, and community standards, the projects can proceed without shifting burdens, while blanket restrictions risk economic and competitive costs. 

Local and state rules (water reporting, noise, full cost recovery, siting limits) are the main response mechanisms.⁠
Foreignpolicy⁠Realclearenergy

In short, right-leaning reporting frames the boom as a private, market-driven AI infrastructure race that the administration is accelerating for competitiveness, with the key policy fights centered on ensuring data centers fully fund their power and resource needs so residents are not left with higher bills or depleted local resources. Outcomes vary sharply by state and locality.

What is the impact on rural area

GROK says:

Rural areas are the primary target for new data centers, creating sharp trade-offs between economic opportunity and pressure on farmland, water, electricity, and community character.

Roughly two-thirds of planned U.S. data centers are slated for rural locations (versus most existing ones in urban areas), drawn by cheaper contiguous land, available transmission, and relatively fewer neighbors or permitting hurdles. Right-leaning coverage (especially WSJ and Fox News) highlights both the potential gains for struggling rural economies and the strong local resistance, particularly from farmers.⁠
WSJ

Land, Farmland, and Agriculture

Data centers permanently convert agricultural land. Examples include Meta acquiring about 2,700 acres of rice fields in rural Louisiana for a massive campus, and utility or developer purchases of grazing land in Montana. Family farms in places like Kentucky have rejected multimillion-dollar offers (one mother-daughter pair turned down roughly $26 million for hundreds of acres held for generations) specifically to keep land in agriculture rather than see it become a hyperscale site. Farmers and ranchers warn of lost productive acreage, upward pressure on land prices that makes it harder for new or expanding operators to buy, and competition for water already heavily used for irrigation. Texas agricultural officials and rural residents have pushed back on projects moving into farm and ranch country, citing risks to the food supply and rural character. Once converted, sites rarely return to farming.
⁠WSJ⁠WSJ

Economic and Fiscal Impacts

Benefits can be substantial where projects succeed and costs are properly managed:

Construction and jobs: 
Multi-year construction employment (hundreds to thousands of workers in skilled trades) plus ongoing roles in operations, maintenance, and security. 

Permanent staffing is lower than construction peaks but often higher-paying than local averages (examples project averages well above regional medians).

Tax revenue: 
Data centers can dominate local tax bases with relatively small land footprints. In Quincy,      Washington—a longstanding farming town that hosted Microsoft and others for ~20 years—data centers have paid a large majority of local taxes.      
Revenue funded a new high school, hospital, library, public safety  facilities, and other infrastructure while supporting population growth and cutting the poverty rate roughly in half. Property tax burdens on      residents dropped relative to what they would have been. Loudoun County, Virginia (a major hub, more exurban), has seen data centers supply around 45% of local tax revenue and generate large estimated savings for homeowners. 
Proposals such as “data center dividends” (sharing a portion of property-tax revenue directly with local households) and state-level plans (e.g., West Virginia dedicating a large share of project revenue to      income-tax reduction) aim to spread benefits more broadly in rural counties.
⁠Fox News
⁠Fox News⁠
Fox News

Caveats noted in coverage include relatively modest permanent headcounts compared with the scale of investment or incentives, and the risk that temporary construction gains do not fully translate into lasting local employment. Some rural areas view the projects as a potential economic lifeline after declines in farming or manufacturing jobs.

Electricity, Water, and Resource Strain

Rural grids and water systems face concentrated demand. A single large campus can consume power comparable to a small city, potentially driving rate increases for residents and farms (where electricity is essential for irrigation, drying, storage, and processing) unless data centers fully cover incremental generation, transmission, and distribution costs. 
This is a central concern in right-leaning reporting and has prompted state-level rules (e.g., in Texas and elsewhere) requiring large loads to pay their own way. Water use for cooling competes with agricultural needs; volumes can be high, though efficiency measures (closed-loop systems, industrial water reuse) can reduce potable draw. Quincy partnered on reuse infrastructure that significantly cut reliance on local groundwater. Dry or irrigation-dependent rural regions are especially sensitive.
⁠WSJ⁠WSJ

Community and Quality-of-Life Effects

Opposition is often intense in rural and farming communities, even in conservative areas. Residents cite noise from cooling equipment, loss of open or agricultural land, changes to the local character, potential utility bill impacts, and limited permanent jobs relative to the footprint. Polling shows substantial rural resistance to nearby projects (though support can be higher for remote sites). Success stories like Quincy are cited by companies and some officials as models of long-term integration when tax revenue is retained locally, energy rates are protected, and water infrastructure is upgraded. Many other rural localities have imposed moratoriums, rejected rezonings, or delayed projects amid public pushback.
⁠WSJ
⁠Fox News

In right-leaning accounts, the rural impact hinges on execution: full cost allocation so residential and farm ratepayers are not subsidizing the centers, retention of tax benefits in the community, careful siting that limits prime farmland loss, and measurable local gains in jobs and infrastructure. Where those conditions hold, some rural towns have seen clear fiscal and economic upside; where they do not, resistance and resource conflicts dominate. Outcomes vary widely by state, utility rules, and local decisions.

How do rural tax revenues compare to urban ones?

GROK says:

Data centers often deliver a larger proportional boost to tax revenue in rural areas than in urban ones, even if absolute dollar amounts are smaller. A single large project (or campus) can represent a transformative share of a small rural county’s budget, while the same facility is a more modest addition to a diversified urban tax base.

Proportional vs. Absolute Impact

Rural and small-town examples: 
In Quincy, Washington (a farming town of roughly 8,000 people that has hosted Microsoft and other      data centers for about 20 years), the facilities pay a very large share of local property taxes—reports put the figure in the range of 57–65% in some measures. This has funded a new high school, hospital, public safety facilities, and other infrastructure, supported population growth, and cut the poverty rate roughly in half. Residents have faced substantially lower      relative property tax burdens than they otherwise would have.⁠
Seattlered

Established (more exurban) hubs:      
Loudoun County, Virginia—the densest data center concentration in the U.S.—generates roughly 40–45% of its total local tax revenue from data centers (on the order of $1.2–1.3 billion annually in recent budgets).      That has supported repeated cuts in residential property tax rates (around 30% over a decade in some accounts) and estimated average homeowner      savings on the order of $5,800 per year relative to a no-data-center scenario. The absolute numbers are far larger because of the sheer volume of facilities.⁠
Fox News

A Bitcoin Policy Institute analysis (covered by Fox News) estimated that a single 1-gigawatt AI data center campus could generate enough surplus property-tax revenue in a typical rural county to support household “dividends” of roughly $4,500–$8,900 per year after funding public services—figures derived in part from Loudoun data scaled to smaller rural tax bases. Louisiana has explored related mechanisms for returning some new data center revenue to residents.
⁠Btcpolicy

Why the Difference

Rural counties start with smaller tax bases, fewer households, and less diversified commercial activity. Adding high-value taxable equipment (servers are often taxed as personal property) and real estate can therefore dominate the local revenue picture and enable lower residential rates or new spending without population growth that strains services. Urban and denser metro areas already have broader residential, commercial, and industrial bases, so the same investment is a smaller percentage of total revenue. They also tend to capture more indirect economic spillovers (suppliers, local spending, specialized labor) because of existing networks.

Right-leaning sources (Fox News, WSJ, Tax Foundation commentary) frequently highlight the property-tax relief potential—especially for homeowners—when facilities pay full freight without heavy abatements. Quincy is often cited as a positive long-running rural model. Some red states (e.g., discussions around Wyoming) view data centers as a way to expand the tax base and ease homeowner burdens.

Important Caveats

Net revenue depends heavily on negotiated incentives, abatements, or payments in lieu of taxes, which are common and can substantially reduce collections in both rural and urban settings. Permanent direct employment is usually modest relative to capital investment (dozens to a few hundred jobs), so the main local fiscal upside is tax revenue rather than payroll. Some research finds metropolitan counties capture larger broader economic gains (jobs, wages, business activity) than pure rural ones because of denser ecosystems. Federal incentives aimed at rural opportunity zones may further encourage rural siting.

In short, rural areas often see a bigger share of their budgets transformed by data centers, while mature urban/exurban clusters generate higher absolute tax dollars and more secondary economic activity. Outcomes vary sharply with local tax structure, abatement deals, and whether ratepayers are protected from related infrastructure costs.

text:
Your Old Electric Car Battery Could Soon Be Powering an AI Data Center, Here’s How | Wonderful Engineering

Redwood Materials is turning retired electric vehicle batteries into energy storage systems designed to help American factories and data centers overcome growing electricity shortages. The initiative aims to give used batteries a second life while helping businesses manage the lengthy delays associated with new grid connections.

The company is working with electric vehicle manufacturer Rivian to deploy second-life battery storage at manufacturing facilities. The approach allows batteries that no longer meet the demands of vehicle use to support stationary power applications, where weight and size are less restrictive.

EV batteries gradually lose capacity through use, but many retain enough energy storage potential to remain useful after retirement. Redwood collects used batteries from Rivian and evaluates whether individual packs can be reused in storage systems or should instead be recycled to recover valuable materials.

Rivian already operates a 10-megawatt-hour second-life battery installation at its manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois. Redwood identifies it as the first installation of its kind at an American automaker’s manufacturing facility. Rivian’s service centers also provide a source of batteries removed during vehicle maintenance and repairs.

However, integrating retired batteries into reliable energy storage systems presents technical challenges. Battery packs differ in chemistry, age, and remaining capacity, making it difficult to operate them together efficiently. Redwood develops its own DC-to-DC converters and control software to manage power across batteries with different characteristics.

The company’s battery recovery operations also provide information about how batteries deteriorate over time, helping engineers determine which packs are suitable for reuse. Developing its own power electronics could offer greater flexibility when designing storage installations and help reduce dependence on equipment with long procurement lead times.

The opportunity extends beyond automotive manufacturing. AI data centers require substantial amounts of electricity, while conventional grid upgrades and electrical equipment can take years to secure. Battery storage can help manage available electricity and provide backup capacity, although it cannot replace the need for sufficient power generation.

Redwood plans to combine its battery systems with solar power and other energy sources to develop microgrids for industrial facilities and data centers. These systems could help businesses meet growing electricity needs while reducing their dependence on new grid connections.

The strategy connects battery recycling with America’s expanding energy infrastructure needs. If the systems prove economically viable at scale, retired EV batteries could become valuable assets for powering the factories and data centers driving the next phase of industrial growth.

text:
On a royal bed at Crúachan, a king and queen began comparing their wealth. By morning, Ireland was on the road to war. 🐂

That's how the Táin Bó Cúailnge opens in the Book of Leinster version, known as Recension II. Ailill tells Medb she is lucky to be a great man's wife. Medb won't have it. She is the daughter of Eochu Feidlech, High King of Ireland, the most generous and the boldest of his six daughters, with her own warband and her own province. She married Ailill because she had asked for something no woman had asked before: a husband without meanness, without jealousy and without fear. And it was Medb who paid the bride-price. So they settle it the way proud rulers do. Everything they own is brought out and counted: cups and vats, rings and gold, cloaks of every colour, sheep, horses and swine. Ram for ram, stallion for stallion, boar for boar, they come out equal.

Then come the cattle. In Ailill's herd stands Finnbennach, the White-Horned bull. He was born to one of Medb's cows, but he would not be counted as a woman's property, so he crossed over to the king's herd. Without a bull to match him, Medb felt as if she owned not a penny. Her herald, Mac Roth, knew of a greater one: the Donn Cúailnge, the Brown Bull of Cooley, kept by Dáire mac Fiachna in Ulster. Medb offered fifty heifers for a year's loan of the bull, with the bull sent back at the end. If Dáire brought it himself, he'd also get land in Mag Aí, a chariot worth thrice seven cumals and Medb's own intimate friendship. Dáire was so pleased that he shook until the seams of the cushions under him burst. He said yes.

That night the messengers drank deep, and one of them boasted that if the bull hadn't been given freely, it would have been taken by force. Dáire's steward overheard. Dáire swore by his gods that the bull would never leave by fair means, and Mac Roth went home with nothing. Medb was not troubled. It was always known, she said, that if he was not given freely he would be taken, and taken he would be. So the hosts began to gather at Crúachan. Recension I skips the pillow talk and opens with the hosting itself. A related tale even says the two bulls were once rival Otherworld swineherds, reborn shape after shape. Their quarrel was never really over.
