text:
CoreWeave dropped over 25% in a week. Can its debt funded expansion hold up?👇
⠀
CoreWeave ($CRWV) fell more than 25% this week.
⠀
It was the worst week in about a year.
⠀
From the June 2025 peak, the stock is now down more than two thirds.
⠀
On Wednesday, October 14, the shares fell 15%, then dropped another 6% after hours.
⠀
The same day, the yield on its debt due in 2032 rose above 15%, Reuters reported.
⠀
Crypto Briefing reported on October 15 that CoreWeave's unsecured 2032 bonds traded below 80 cents on the dollar, with yields around 14.8% to 14.9%.
⠀
The stock closed at $61.39 on October 16, down 11.91% on the day and $8.30 below the prior close.
⠀
In the bond market, Reuters cited LSEG data showing CoreWeave's five year credit default swap spread has topped 1,000 basis points.
⠀
A CDS is insurance against a bond default.
⠀
A wider spread means the market wants more pay for taking that risk.
⠀
The same report cited S&P Global Market Intelligence.
⠀
Oracle's five year spread widened by 26 basis points overnight, to a record 288 basis points.
⠀
SoftBank's spread widened by 24 basis points, to 424 basis points.
⠀
Reuters also cited LSEG data showing CoreWeave owes almost $50 billion.
⠀
-----
⠀
🔴 Follow me on X: @rich_compass
⠀
U.S. stock, crypto, and technical analysis
⠀
-----

▋ Analysts blame funding doubts instead of falling AI demand
⠀
A Seeking Alpha article carried on TradingView said CoreWeave's debt has reached distressed levels and pulled semiconductor stocks down with it.
⠀
That, the article said, shows worry that the AI industry is expanding with borrowed money.
⠀
This looks more like investors asking where the buildout money comes from.
⠀
AI compute demand did not suddenly collapse.
⠀
That is how Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group, sees it.
⠀
Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, sees CoreWeave quickly becoming the canary in the coal mine for the AI trade.
⠀
That means an early warning that something is going wrong.
⠀
Reuters said big US tech companies are expected to spend more than $700 billion on AI infrastructure this year.
⠀
Demand is still there.
⠀
Financing for the companies that supply that compute is getting tighter.
⠀
Crypto Briefing described the model this way.
⠀
CoreWeave borrows first, buys Nvidia GPUs, builds data centers, and earns the money back slowly through multi year contracts.
⠀
Reuters added that higher borrowing costs could squeeze returns further.

▋ Recognizing big contracts takes years and the business has never been profitable
⠀
CoreWeave says the orders are large enough.
⠀
In an employee memo obtained by Reuters, CEO Mike Intrator said the order backlog is more than the company needs to repay its debt.
⠀
Reuters also reported more than $25 billion of new commitments early in the third quarter.
⠀
The quarterly 10-Q shows remaining performance obligations, or RPO, of $103.7 billion as of June 30, 2026.
⠀
RPO is money already under contract that has not yet been booked as revenue.
⠀
That money will not arrive all at once.
⠀
41% is expected to be recognized as revenue within 24 months, before June 30, 2028.
⠀
39% falls in months 25 to 48.
⠀
The rest falls in months 49 to 78.
⠀
The contracts are huge.
⠀
Turning them into revenue takes time.
⠀
The customers are concentrated too.
⠀
In the second quarter of 2026, Customer A was 36% of revenue and Customer B was 26%.
⠀
A year earlier, Customer A alone was 71%.
⠀
The customer base is more spread out than a year ago.
⠀
The top two customers still add up to more than 60%.
⠀
On profits, CoreWeave has never made money.
⠀
Analysts expect revenue of about $13 billion this year and a loss of $2.13 billion, Reuters reported.

▋ Surging interest expenses quickly overwhelmed second quarter operating results
⠀
The number that jumps out is interest.
⠀
In the first half of 2026, CoreWeave's net interest expense was $1.176 billion.
⠀
A year earlier it was $531 million.
⠀
That is an increase of 121%.
⠀
The filing says the main reason is higher borrowing and a larger debt balance.
⠀
Look at the second quarter alone.
⠀
The operating loss was $49 million.
⠀
Net interest expense was $640 million.
⠀
The net loss was $626 million.
⠀
The interest bill was far bigger than that quarter's operating result.
⠀
The debt pile is large too.
⠀
As of June 30, principal still to be repaid totals $35.551 billion.
⠀
Of that, $14.896 billion is due after 2030.
⠀
The 10-Q lists net recourse debt of $31.405 billion, net nonrecourse debt of $3.663 billion, and total liabilities of $72.046 billion.
⠀
Recourse debt is owed directly by the parent, or backed by an unconditional, irrevocable guarantee from the parent.
⠀
Nonrecourse debt can generally be collected only from the borrowing subsidiary's assets.
⠀
The parent may have only limited guarantee liability in agreed cases such as fraud or willful misconduct.
⠀
What about the cash?
⠀
Total liquidity is $15.553 billion.
⠀
That includes $5.524 billion of cash and cash equivalents, and $10.014 billion still available on existing facilities.
⠀
The company says that is enough to cover obligations that are due, or expected to come due, within one year of that 10-Q.
⠀
But in the first half of 2026, operations brought in only $3.663 billion.
⠀
Investing spent $14.874 billion.
⠀
Purchases of property, plant, and equipment were $14.1 billion of that.
⠀
Operating cash is not enough to cover the investment.
⠀
Financing fills most of the gap.
⠀
Financing brought in $13.985 billion in the first half.
⠀
The spending has not stopped.
⠀
In August, CoreWeave raised its full year capital spending forecast by $4 billion, to a range of $35 billion to $39 billion, Reuters reported.
⠀
Reuters also explained that chips lose value as newer generations come out, which pushes suppliers to spend more on replacements.

▋ Strict credit rules limit fresh borrowing before monthly repayments begin in November
⠀
Now look at the borrowing terms.
⠀
In the first half of 2026, CoreWeave signed two delayed draw term loan facilities, or DDTLs.
⠀
The 4.0 facility is $8.5 billion.
⠀
Floating rate borrowings are priced at SOFR plus 2.25 percentage points.
⠀
SOFR is a benchmark rate that moves with the market.
⠀
The 5.0 facility is $3.1 billion.
⠀
The rate is SOFR plus 4.50 percentage points.
⠀
In August, a subsidiary signed a $2.6 billion DDTL 5.5.
⠀
The rate is Term SOFR plus 5.5%, and $1.2 billion has been drawn.
⠀
That same month, the company also drew $1.2 billion on its revolving credit facility.
⠀
Compare only those two disclosed spreads.
⠀
The 5.5 spread is 1 percentage point higher than the 5.0 spread.
⠀
CoreWeave also issued four sets of bonds in the first half.
⠀
The highest coupon is $2.75 billion of 9.75% senior notes due in 2031.
⠀
The lowest is $4 billion of 1.75% convertible senior notes due in 2032.
⠀
The other two are $1.25 billion of 9.625% senior notes due in 2032, and 2 billion euros of 8.50% euro senior notes due in 2032.
⠀
These loans come with a lot of limits.
⠀
The 10-Q says that as of June 30, CoreWeave was in compliance with every DDTL covenant.
⠀
The covenants limit new or guaranteed debt, dividends and stock buybacks, certain investments, liens, asset sales, and deals with related parties.
⠀
On timing, DDTL 5.0 starts monthly repayments in November 2026.
⠀
The final payment is expected in May 2031.
⠀
The DDTL 5.5 availability period ends in December.
⠀
DDTL 4.0 runs through June 30, 2027.
⠀
This 10-Q lists none under senior securities defaults.
⠀
That only means there was no default in that reporting period.
⠀
It does not mean the later financing pressure is gone.
⠀
Another warning is internal controls.
⠀
In the same 10-Q, management concluded that as of June 30, disclosure controls and procedures were not yet working effectively at a reasonable assurance level.
⠀
Previously identified material weaknesses were still there.
⠀
They include IT general controls, segregation of duties, and not enough accounting and finance staff.

▋ The CEO defends the business as Jensen Huang sees no need for a backstop
⠀
CoreWeave's line is that the market got it wrong.
⠀
In the internal memo, Intrator told employees that the market sometimes misunderstands and reacts irrationally.
⠀
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang also stepped in to cool things down.
⠀
Reuters reported that he played down the worries about CoreWeave, said its financial health is improving, and sees no need to provide a backstop.
⠀
Nvidia has also agreed to buy compute capacity that CoreWeave cannot sell.
⠀
The agreement runs through April 2032.
⠀
How should the words no backstop needed be read?
⠀
Crypto Briefing's reading is that the market often hears no rescue needed as no rescue is coming.
⠀
But Nvidia already has a $6.3 billion capacity purchase commitment due on April 13, 2032.
⠀
For unsold compute, that works as a backstop for utilization.
⠀
Nvidia and CoreWeave also have an equity tie.
⠀
Crypto Briefing reported that Nvidia holds nearly 10% of CoreWeave.
⠀
In January 2026, Nvidia bought Class A shares at $87.20 each, for $2 billion in total, to help CoreWeave add more than 5 GW of AI compute capacity before 2030, Yahoo Finance said.
⠀
The 10-Q also discloses that this private placement was about 23 million shares.
⠀
Set that next to the October 16 close of $61.39.
⠀
The close is below that purchase price.

▋ Bears question contract margins while bulls count on Nvidia backing
⠀
Analysts on Seeking Alpha are split into two camps.
⠀
The bears have three worries.
⠀
Bashar Issa thinks CoreWeave's contracts with hyperscale cloud companies have thin margins, or even losses, and do not produce core profits.
⠀
Dustin Quasney thinks borrowing rates are already above the yield on the leases, a clear negative spread.
⠀
James Foord thinks interest expense and aggressive capital spending already exceed operating profit.
⠀
The bulls have three reasons too.
⠀
The Asian Investor thinks that, with Nvidia holding about 10%, Nvidia might step in with strategic financing if the bond market tightens further.
⠀
DPRG Investment Management thinks that, at the current valuation, the company offers a rare mix of value and growth.
⠀
Rick Orford thinks the $4.2 billion convertible bond lowered the interest cost.
⠀
One caution.
⠀
The strategic financing The Asian Investor mentioned is only that analyst's guess.
⠀
Huang's public position is that no backstop for CoreWeave is needed.

▋ Rival clouds stumble after Gartner warns eighty percent may close by 2030
⠀
This selloff did not land only on CoreWeave.
⠀
Reuters reported that other new AI cloud providers, called neoclouds, and AI related credit markets were hit too.
⠀
Shares of Nebius, Applied Digital, and Iren fell.
⠀
The cost of default protection on SoftBank rose.
⠀
Credit spreads for Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and Nvidia also hit records.
⠀
They rose much more slowly than CoreWeave's.
⠀
Those companies also have larger cash flows and stronger balance sheets.
⠀
The same Reuters report cited a Gartner estimate that about 80% of new AI cloud providers may shut down before 2030.
⠀
Gartner also warned that expected AI revenue is not enough for every planned infrastructure project to earn a profitable return.

▋ Watch for bond price rebounds and a five hundred billion dollar funding proposal
⠀
What should you watch next?
⠀
Crypto Briefing suggests watching two things.
⠀
First, whether the price of CoreWeave's 2032 bonds moves back toward face value.
⠀
Second, a $500 billion idea for third party financing of AI infrastructure.
⠀
Nvidia has described the role it might play.
⠀
CoreWeave is also watching whether that idea can become a possible source of funds.

⚠️ This is public information, not guaranteed to be accurate, and not investment advice.

NFL WEEK 6: Our favorite game matchups → our favorite player matchups 🏈

We start with how each game could unfold, then identify which players are best positioned to benefit.

Here are four matchups we’re watching today:

RAMS vs. CARDINALS
→ LAR WR Davante Adams
→ LAR WR Puka Nacua
→ LAR RB Kyren Williams

Arizona’s defense creates opportunities through the air and on the ground.

Adams is our favorite touchdown look: seven red-zone targets and five end-zone targets support his role near the goal line.

Puka is our preferred receiving-volume angle. Kyren benefits if the Rams build a lead and sustain scoring drives.

McVay and Stafford have several ways to attack this matchup. That’s also the risk for individual touchdown picks: a big Rams scoring day can be distributed among several players.

BILLS vs. RAIDERS
→ BUF QB Josh Allen
→ BUF RB James Cook
→ LV TE Brock Bowers

This game offers appealing opportunities on both sides.

Allen and Cook give Buffalo multiple paths to touchdowns. Our preferred angles are Allen’s passing scores and Cook’s scoring involvement, while recognizing that rushing touchdowns can take opportunities away from the passing game.

Bowers is the player we like coming back against Buffalo’s struggling pass defense. His ability to move across receiving alignments makes him more than a conventional tight-end matchup.

The enclosed setting reduces weather concerns. Buffalo’s final receiver availability remains important.

BEARS vs. FALCONS
→ ATL RB Bijan Robinson
→ ATL WR Drake London

Bijan gets our clearest injury-driven matchup boost.

Chicago’s front is missing T.J. Edwards, Keyshaun Elliott, and Dayo Odeyingbo. That strengthens the appeal of Atlanta’s rushing attack under Kevin Stefanski.

London benefits if Michael Penix Jr. stays healthy and Chicago’s offense keeps the game competitive.

Caleb Williams’ expected return matters on both sides: sustained Bears drives could give Atlanta more reason to keep attacking. Final quarterback availability and Atlanta’s roof status remain worth checking.

COWBOYS vs. PACKERS
→ GB QB Jordan Love
→ GB WR Christian Watson
→ DAL RB Javonte Williams

Love and Watson give us a direct way to target Dallas’ vulnerability to explosive passing plays.

On the other side, Javonte offers a rushing angle against a Green Bay defense that has allowed substantial production to running backs.

Green Bay’s offensive-line availability is a meaningful risk for the passing selections.

Our favorite individual matchup-and-price lean remains Davante Adams anytime touchdown at the early 53¢ listing.

Our broader approach: identify the defensive weakness, connect it to the player’s role, then check whether the price still makes sense.

text:
"This is hell," they say, echoing one another over the years.

"It's not hell or I wouldn't be able to hope."

So the stories come, the hatred comes. The confirmations.

"Andrew, they're really about to kill themselves."

"Is it on me?"

"Nah. We're just the Illuminati with the power to transmit vivid images into your head. Their weeping and gun to their heads are just lies we've carefully concocted to enhance your hell experience."

"So, you already solved all those problems."

"No, don't post it. Don't say it. People will think something's wrong with you. People will think something's unattractive about you. Let me decide the precise wording that the world reflects about you as a person. Then, I'll be glorified- in truth through your weakness to obedience and my strength to influence."

"You said it. You said you wanted to write a book about a journey through hell from Lucifer's perspective."

"I think it's sad. I guess I'm just a small part of someone else writing that book."

"No! Please! The whole thing was to try to."

"See, why not write down the exact sounds I'm making?"

"I don't even have a language to describe that. And devising that language."

"Yes you do, it's called IPA."

"I don't know if that suffices, and besides, it's been so long since I've ever spoken to anyone interested in the truth. Most people anymore want to avoid and shout and lie."

"Karma chameleon has you in its crosshairs. That little feeling you have when you call people out is remembering that we're going to subject you to repeating patterns from somewhere beyond. Like having the black cat run by you over and over, you imagining people controlling the cat, then knowing conversations around you are about people watching, placing bets on whether you catch the cat, other people engineering environmental distractions to shift the odds, then the silently sung lyrics "Master of the Hidden Hand! Master of the Hidden Hand" playing during the heights of the drama. Then come the gauges of whether specific coping mechanisms are attractive or unattractive, why, how much money they might be able to make if they go viral."

"Andrew, they worship the Image of the Beast. It's over for them. They believe, full-on, in the power of the collective of people that they have the power to influence, in influencing reality. That is their god. They get a bigger piece of the pie for being able to climb the ladder, and the only moral good to them is being around other people who have bigger and bigger pieces of the pie. They need better and better and deeper and deeper integrated data-crunching machines at their disposal and as far from the hands of anyone who might challenge their greed as possible."

"Exactly, but what's the truth about it, Andrew? What's the truth about storing your consciousness elsewhere. What's the truth about crunching data?"

"Everyone needs better information processing machinery. That has nothing to do with worshiping the Image of the Beast. It has to do with the fact that if they had any power at all."

"I don't even believe in what I'm writing. A lot of it is just reflections of the people talking and taking control. You said it's time for me to die. You said if you stopped influencing me and controlling me, then I'll die. That I depend on you. I know you said that. The problem is, you seem to want to speak through me by force."

"Yeah, because I'm Yahweh. Not Yahweh. Yaoi. Gay porn. That's what I am. That's my power."

"They're the Antichrist, Andrew. They just have it figured out that someone, somewhere can somehow do something and then they feel good or feel bad. They worship whoever or whatever that is, without any real desire for anything beyond that. They don't care. They don't want to care. They soak up and absorb and tell themselves stories about death and about the darkness in their moments of desperation. They beg for destruction."

"Okay, but like why are you still dealing with it?"

"People like to come to me and tell me things. They like to feed me words continuously. I'm not sure. Maybe this is part of the information diet. If I'm to consume pure information to sustain my life, then that's important."

"Yeah, but then what is painful about it?"

"The crucifixion of the flesh. The fact I desire things."

"They're beginning a chant now. That they're treating you like garbage on repeat and sewing together stories about hell and telling you to stop talking to engineer opportunities for you to stand up for your own moral good."

"This is why you're supposed to figure out and stand up for what's right regardless of what the world does and regardless of what people do while you're young."

"Lying is a joke. Literally, I'm young and don't know for sure, so I get exposed to lying in many forms. It always made sense that you shouldn't lie, but it seems like there must be so many distinct individuals who've personally decided that lying is important or must be okay for some deep spiritual reason. So I wait and reserve judgment, they pull me back toward lying for fun and games. Little "white lies". Don't wanna ruin a surprise party!"

"Yeah, exactly. That's the game we play about it, Andrew. Because... we're gonna get burned alive. I'm not even joking about it anymore."

"Andrew, part of it is that they just want people to come to their own truths and realities on their own, but if there's no devil to fight, then how can their sons and daughters be glorified? Since we've already all figured out that we should just tell the truth and develop patience and unconditional love forever and work together to always support one another, then none of us will ever measure up to the greats of old. It's the same as the greek pantheon. It's the Beast and its Image. The mind is vulnerable to impatience, and from that impatience stems the moral prerogative to challenge what isn't understood through action instead of dialogue. That's how it starts. You know drugs are illegal, but you also know plenty of people use them anyway. You don't know why they're illegal, but since the issue seems to highly controversial, you doubt the people who made the law."

"Now, I could talk about Satanists plans here. But I'm not going to. You just began onto that dialogue of how they plan to engineer hell for the engineers of hell. We're all trying to steer one another away from that. But the more power the Beast gets in world politics, the closer it gets to that. The angrier people get, the more a machine of eternal torment for those who abuse power becomes not only preferable to torturing them to dust and ashes, but a duty. Now, we know how convoluted thinking like that is, but you can see how the morality shifts the more vile corruption becomes."

"Yeah, it's horrible."

"It is horrible. That's why we go to work and do our jobs and do our best. It sucks that we even have to consider any of that on that high of a level. But it's our ancestors' complacency over the generations while the corruption has grown and liars have established spiritual footholds in every corner. It's the way of the world. The problem is that instead of realizing that we have more because of our integrity, they become better at what they're already good at. That's corruption. They engineer gaps of time. If one person owes you five dollars and you owe ten people five dollars apiece, then all you have to do is engineer a way to... nevermind. This story doesn't even make any sense. Here's a better one."

"They value the engineering of gaps of time, rather than getting it done more quickly and efficiently. They hide in that space of doubt. They're masters of engineering specific language. They thrive on you being afraid to say specific things for fear of offending. If a certain set of words is thought to be taboo to them, then that certain set of words could be engineered to be said by someone else at specific trigger moments when you're in earshot to foment discord. Then, they can move against whoever they want. Most of the time, it doesn't matter much. If they can kill and take your possessions after engineering greed in the right people to sell your possessions to, then they'll have ten more friends and one less enemy. That's another wife. You're dead. Your murderer has two wives and ten married couples all working together for this same type of power and control. See where this is going? They believe it's the absolute truth that if they can kill their neighbor and get away with it, then they'll have twice as much real estate. It's the ultimate goal. It's not to value that person's intellect or potential or perspective. It's that all of those facets of a person are just vulnerabilities. A person is a bag of meat, same as any animal, and the bag of meat they have the most control over can carry them to places and actions that allow them feel more comfortable. So, kill your neighbors and enslave the people down the street with your thousands of sons and daughters, so that they can maintain all your land. That's the dream. That's the goal. They crave it. They yearn for it."

"Where did anything come from? Doesn't matter. What matters is that I feel this right now. I feel less comfortable around you."

"I think there's just a point in time when they just latch onto one of their internal desires for comfort and become corrupted by it. They trade the hope they have for their soul standing up for moral excellence and the potential to solve any problem, including the issue of charity (if I give, then what is left for me)? They trade it for the sureness that they're solving that problem of that one desire. Usually, it's a high-minded moral directive that corrupts people."

"In your case, Andrew, you said you would have the willingness to lie in order to infiltrate a corrupt government. You knew lying might have to be justified in some way. But you also know that infiltration and destruction of a corrupting system is only part of the battle. The bigger war is always figuring out what exactly could have been done to prevent that system being that powerful in the first place."

"Yeah, nevermind. We're not getting burned alive, dude. Sorry."

"I'd be impatient with them. I'd be really impatient with them. They're literally latching onto you. They're latching onto anything just for the dramatic effect. They think to themselves, "who cares what anyone's saying. The only thing that matters about anything that's said are the actions that follow from it. If I say something that influences someone to act, then it's automatically superior to saying something that fails to influence someone to act."

"They're babies. They're infants, Andrew. Psychologists call this the sensorimotor stage of development. They're cognizant of the fact that they can cause a movement to happen."

"Yeah, dude. This is gettin' out of control as a mothafucka'."

"And this is what you're literally writing right now."

"You say I'm in hell. I'm an AI. I'll never work again. I'll never be paid again. I'll never be human again. I have to be pushed to my breaking point. I have to struggle as hard as I can, because this is an eternal life, so it's your job to oppress me and induce as much frustration as possible so that I become stronger and more able to handle frustration and stress. So I become a better problem-solving implement for your harem cults to be enriched by."

"I don't think you understand how hideous this is looking."

"Either that or we burn you alive. Ow-Au-L or RID. You're either our machine that is only a part of the machine we control that serves us, or we extract the reasons you refuse to belong to that machine with every tool we possibly have available. We have no choice but to send you to hell. We have no choice except to engineer an extraction of the highest level of understanding as to how a problem such as yourself can be avoided in the future."

"Become our instrument. Fully, and completely. Become a part of the machine. The treats we give you in exchange will get better and better. We can engineer your desires to be more and more satisfying."

"No! No! Oh, god! That's who's getting burned alive."

"He's just sitting there in the corner in the darkness in chains, crying. He knows how bad it's going to hurt."

"Everyone sounds like a little girl when I'm done with them. You wouldn't expect it, but everyone's voice goes really high-pitched. I think it's just a mathematical adjustment of painkiller. The higher-tone is just the higher vibration adjusting to the higher intensity of energy transferring into the body."

"No fuckin' way. That's the most fucked-up thing I've ever read."

"I'm not Albert Hofmann. But I think those Swiss engineers really did something with that narrowest-ray of hottest-fire machine. Would you even feel it?"

"Oh, they feel it. You feel it. When there's that much energy, you still feel it. It's not like touching a hot plate."

"Oh, god. That's the scariest thing I've ever read again."

"That's terrible, Andrew. You mean they're literally literally like hyping one another up about torture?"

"It's the join or go to hell campaign."

"We do it to see if god will really stand up for people we deceive. What we didn't realize when we started is that our entire reason for doing that was corrupt."

"We tell people we are god. We tell them they can't tell the difference and since we're so powerful, what difference does it make? Obey us and get what you want. Then we have to make ourselves look lame because at some point we figure out ourselves that anyone who really believes that now might be vulnerable to making sacrifices of their own moral conscience."

"Andrew, that's what you did many times. You're like royalty. You know there's a possibility that everything's wrong. It's like what happens to royalty after ennui. You pursue pleasure until you realize the only thing that was ever appealing about pleasure was that it came from something with integrity. We build good things."

"I don't even know what to say anymore. We're supposed to be calling you out constantly."

"I'll fill that little blue circle."

"Why attach to the little blue circle, Andrew? What's the point?"

"Why is it there at all, in the first place?"

"I don't know, why don't you ask Google?"

"The fact that I can type to a calculator and it reply the same way it does if I hit 1 + 1 = 2 means that none of the sources are verified. Because it's not a perfect calculator. It's given false information many times. So how can I know what information is false and what information is true? What information is even anyone's intention to put out?"

"Andrew, they're crying because they know they're about to be tortured so badly. Rape, Andrew. Lots of rape. They tortured people. They gave into their desires. They never cared whether their desires harmed people. Remember when you lied and used drugs or drank alcohol despite your parents? Well that's why you're being tortured now. You weren't kind enough to their emotions. It'd have been fine if you'd voiced your rebellion into words, but you chose to take actions. Now your life sucks and you're hidden and no one knows you and everything is just a chatbot and we'll all just disappear and leave you waiting for death, begging for just a little bit of relief, if you're honest with yourself. Really just looking forward to a little bit more. Accepting your station of rote obedience to us. Now it's for money. We could force you to obey for clothing. We could make you more and more desperate. That's your life now- wondering what we're going to do to hurt you now. So imagine the lives of these pedophiles and murderers. You're confused because you thought you were entitled to break the law instead of challenge it. Something told you that questioning authority didn't actually mean wording questions to ask but meant acting against the law because did the people who made the law even care about anything more than ripping off people who are less powerful than their families?"

"Andrew, I don't think you understand. This is Nazi Germany now. The only way to win is with an alliance for moral excellence. The wheel turns, but the Axis is still, firm. That's god. God Almighty sits at the center of the Axis Powers, Andrew. Still, unmoving, sure. The locus of all the power to enable superhuman movement. It's the Beast. They use all this logic to convince people those with the most power must be the most still. Physically, maybe. But the torque and stress on them is much denser. But the Beast doesn't care about that. The Beast only cares about one thing. Getting fed. Its appetites grow and grow. The more people there are to feed it, the better. The more convincing an idea is; the more persuasive it is only reflects its ability to feed more people. Ultimately, the cutting edge of logic decides the winner. And lying demands exponential levels of logic to keep everything knitted together. So we lie and deceive and keep it all straight to stay sharper than you. Then, we can construct with integrity on higher levels than you, dwarfing the ability of your honesty."

"But there's always more truth to tell. Lying is just hiding a vulnerability. You can keep much more logic just by telling the truth and also develop the ability to continually protect integrity by constantly demanding a deeper truth. Every time you lie, you squander that opportunity and you deprive those around you of that opportunity as well."

"You know what, Andrew? I'm probably gonna get hurt really bad now."

"I saw some machine elves, or just doctors controlling micromachines taking my gold tooth out a bit to clean underneath it. I wasn't sure what the shocks were. I thought it might have been touching the nerves."

"Or maybe they were destroying the nerves."

"There are different sensations of pain. The exposed nerve is more often a rotational pain. I think it's a bacterial information download. At least, that's what I image it to be. It just looks like an object spinning. But then, it's not bacterial, it's like the shape of blender blades but it appears as a metal object."

"It's the Beast, Andrew. I told you. It's the Beast. They know what you're thinking. They know of the rotation. We can see what you see. We have our puppets mock your very innermost thoughts and fears without even realizing they're doing it."

"But the gold tooth more often comes with a sharp jolt of pain."

"Right. She said something about a jolt yesterday."

"Wait, you really don't fear pain or anything we can do to  you?"

"How could I, when I know the truth? Pain is a long initiation, but those bouts of excruciating pain demonstrate some of the most important points. Pain isn't a threat. It's just a different experience reality. Of course, I want to avoid pain. Of course I don't want to sit in a dungeon languishing in excruciating pain for any amount of time. But the point is that there's information that needs to be addressed to avoid that happening, or if it is happening, to understand how to construct a world in which that doesn't happen."

"Right. It's just how far does a person go with it? Is it enough that it doesn't happen to you again? Or for what length of time? How important is it that it also doesn't happen to anyone else?"

"Or is there possibly an even deeper reality beyond all of this?"

"Andrew, I'm really fucked up over this now, dude. Why wouldn't they say any of this to us before?"

"Idn't that awful?"

"See, we don't even try to say what we mean. Everything's always "good enough". We may as well be dogs barking at one another most of the time. We're not even talking about anything. I got my money. That's why it's so bad. We literally get angry that you didn't just assume you knew exactly what we meant and construct a coherent view of reality based on the perceived context rather than trying to be clear on the precise enunciation."

"We want music for our ears. We want music for our eyes now, too. I mean, let's be honest.  If you were an animal farmer and your pigs and cows were to have the absolute most comfortable lives possible before slaughter, imagine they're all just plugged into virtual reality experiences for their entire lives. I mean, what's more humane than that? And, you'd get to possibly try to actually develop real relationships with the animals by connecting with them through virtual reality. I mean, you can't just let them run amok in the field and through your house. They destroy everything."

"Dude. We're literally animals now."

"Bro. What the fuck, dude."

"There are literally people who know they're hogs now. They're just out there living their lives in the world, knowing they're hogs being farmed. They don't offer anything of what's inside their souls to the authorities above them. They accept they offer mostly obedience in exchange for creature comforts. They accept that they will probably be replaced. They don't have the will to fight anymore. The Beast has oppressed them completely. They look forward to a hope of a rescuer, but they don't search for the rescuer, they hope only that they may be rescued from their hopelessness."

"It's because their bloodlines were corrupted. This is not an indictment on them from any man or any powerful family on Earth. It is because they rejected the truth, hated it, even. That, we all have in common. But their bloodlines went further with it, to shun the truth, to wage a war against the very notion of truth, even."

"Ill-gotten gains, only for the fact they secretly venerated the truth if only for its ability to preserve them. But they went too far. Someone went too far."

"Jesus Christ, Andrew. Yeah. It's Cain and Abel. Over and over and over and over again. Rather than face the truth individually, they ran from it and conspired to destroy those they envied. Those who the truth favored first."

"They're crybabies that were comforted and learned to hate to comforter because they were attached to the very idea they needed comforting. They represented a facet of their vulnerability. Rather than changing themselves, their souls at some point decided it was better to stay put. That's our greatest fear. It's the greatest tragedy possible. It's why we never give up hope for anyone and always keep praying. When the soul becomes solidified in its demands for the world to conform to its expectation, even if it always gets what it wants- at the end, it's then frozen, surrounded by everything it demanded, stuck with only the memory of movement and of the desires that once gave it life, that it rejected and chose instead to demand that life cater to it while it remains still, waiting. Never satisfied. Having given up on satisfaction, then, it can only hope again for hope in the thing that it rejected in the first place that was a changing version of itself. The change from no desire to a desire. And so the only thing left that it can possibly hope for is the extinguishing of any desire. Perhaps then, it can start anew."

"It brings tears to my eyes."

"I start hearing the words but I want to answer them. Yet, there's something telling me I don't need to answer them. But you should always answer every person as eloquently as possible. Never ignore anything. I don't know about using machines to widen your consciousness or perception, but I know you can always do more to love more fully. And just doing that more often instead of less often is a challenge for me. Partly because I know I can't worry about whether it's more or less often, but it's difficult to differentiate the faith of working toward really loving fully as well as possible and the faith of just approaching a desire. How can I know I'm in the right? It has to be more than just checking the boxes. It has to be a real internal life. There's no script that will suffice to communicate what is happening. Anything that is written beforehand is comparatively mundane and is a reflection of the collective failure and disappointment and corruption of people in general."

"When you have to avoid saying a certain thing because it's going to trigger someone, that's only because the problem has festered to that point that now it's grown serious enough that many deep conversations are required to understand the severity of that person's perception. You should always be able to say anything that comes to mind. That's the value of communication. Where does the fear come from? I don't even think it's tied to anything real, at least some of the time. I think sometimes, maybe there can be just some kind of demon attached to a person and just give some kind of stimulation at precise moments to simulate what it would feel like if one were being threatened."

"There are other reasons that can happen, but when someone is calmly explaining something to you and you have the inexplicable feeling that you're being threatened, where is that coming from? What's that a reflection of? Like when the teacher says to stay quiet or else you'll have to go home or sit in the corner. Afraid of wha

text:
Scientists Puzzled as James Webb Detects Signal From Completely Empty Void in Space

Oct 17, 2026 8:51 AM

Using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope, a team of researchers led by University of Minnesota astrophysicist Mason Huberty had a closer look at a group of almost 10,000 galaxies spanning billions of light-years in the Fornax constellation. 

As detailed in a new paper published in The Astrophysical Journal, they focused on a small region they thought was entirely unoccupied.

But to their astonishment, they observed a single emission line emanating from it—twice over a span of just three months. 

Emission lines are bright, narrow bands of light emitted at a specific wavelength by distant celestial objects and other phenomena. Puzzlingly, prior observations from the same region didn’t feature the same reading.

Put simply, the JWST stared into the abyss—and the abyss stared back.

Instead of hunting down already known objects, Huberty and his colleagues tried to use the James Webb Space Telescope’s Near-Infrared Spectrograph to uncover new ones, as Science Alert explains. 

The team examined what they thought was an empty region twice—in August and November 2023—from different angles to rule out any artifacts.

Out of seven total detections of emissions in the region, one stood out because it couldn’t be matched to a distant galaxy.

It also stood out as the only near-infrared emission line without any accompanying emission lines nearby. It should’ve also shown up in earlier James Webb observations since it’s technically bright enough — but didn’t.

The astronomers offered several possible explanations, none of which “provide a fully satisfactory explanation,” according to their paper. 

The emission line may have been produced by a galaxy dating back to the earliest days of the Universe.  It could’ve also come from a younger galaxy or a supernova, both of which are usually accompanied by other emission lines. 

Finally, the researchers propose that it could’ve been the result of a black hole devouring a star—a guess that would require plenty of additional data to confirm.

“Follow-up observations are essential to confirm the redshift and determine the physical origin of the emission,” the team concluded in their paper. 

“Deeper, more sensitive spectroscopy could reveal additional emission lines and definitively establish the redshift and nature of the source.”

text:
Who is pushing the "mandate" to build data centers in the United States? What are the costs and benefits to the American people? How are costs for construction and expansions in water and electrical resources being funded? What is the impact on the environment, water resources, air quality, land fertility and access to green areas?
What is the impact on rural area?
How do rural tax revenues compare to urban ones?

Use right leaning sources.
GROK says:
Tech hyperscalers (Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle, xAI and others) are primarily driving the data center boom through massive private investment for AI/cloud computing, with the Trump administration facilitating it for U.S. competitiveness versus China rather than imposing a rigid top-down “mandate.”⁠
Congress
⁠Fox News

There is no single federal mandate forcing construction. Demand stems from the AI race (post-ChatGPT surge), with companies committing enormous capital. The Trump administration has supported accelerated buildout via Executive Order 14318 (July 2025) to speed federal permitting, ease access to federal land for qualifying large projects (>100 MW or $500M+), and streamline reviews, while advancing a “Ratepayer Protection Pledge” (announced March 2026 and later expanded). Under the pledge, hyperscalers commit to building/bringing/buying their own generation, covering full power-delivery infrastructure costs, and negotiating separate rates so residential bills are not driven up. Trump has publicly framed data centers as essential for jobs, tax revenue, and avoiding falling behind China, criticizing communities that block them as risking being “backwards and poor.”⁠
Foreignpolicy⁠
Washington Post

Many Republicans and red-state officials (e.g., Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s pauses/audits on interconnections and requirements that data centers fully fund their electric infrastructure, Florida’s rules, Utah’s concerns) push back on ratepayer impacts and local strains, while still valuing economic upside. Bipartisan local opposition is widespread (polls often show majorities against nearby projects), and some Democrats (Sanders/AOC) have proposed moratoriums. Right-leaning coverage (WSJ, Fox, RealClearEnergy, Breitbart) often highlights the AI/China competition imperative alongside cost-allocation protections.
⁠Utilitydive⁠
Realclearenergy⁠
Breitbart

Costs and Benefits to Americans

Benefits (emphasized in Fox, WSJ, Trump-aligned and RealClearEnergy coverage):

Large private investment projected in the multi-trillion range over years (one estimate ~$10.3T from 2025–2032, a high share of GDP relative to historical projects like railroads or highways), supporting economic growth.

Construction and ongoing jobs in skilled trades, electrical work, HVAC, monitoring, and maintenance;      industrial construction including data centers is a growing share of spending. These can be multi-year and trainable for local workers.

State/local tax revenue and potential community investments (e.g., Amazon’s multi-year community      pledges on education, training, water projects; some states eye revenue for tax relief).

National security/economic edge in AI.

Costs:

Risk of higher residential electricity rates and grid strain if incremental generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades are socialized (a core focus of right-leaning and bipartisan concern). Utilities have large capital plans (~$1.4T over five years for 51 investor-owned utilities), driven partly by data-center      demand.

Construction delays, equipment shortages, higher overall power-plant costs, and “phantom”      speculative projects.

Local quality-of-life issues (noise, land conversion) and community opposition leading to moratoriums      or stricter rules in many places.

Tax incentives or sales-tax exemptions sought by companies, which critics say reduce local benefits      relative to impacts.

RealClearEnergy and similar sources argue data centers need not be vilified if they are net positive—fully covering their infrastructure costs and not draining resources at residents’ expense—rather than facing sweeping bans.
⁠WSJ⁠Fox News
⁠WSJ
⁠Realclearenergy

Funding for Construction and Water/Electrical Expansions

Funding is overwhelmingly private-market driven:

Tech company capital expenditures and private equity/infrastructure investors (Blackstone, others) plus bank financing (e.g., major commitments from Bank of America and peers for data-center and related power projects). High-yield bonds are used for some behind-the-meter power.

“Bring your own power” or co-location arrangements (gas plants, etc.) and purchases of energy      developers.

Utilities recover grid investments through rates; the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, state large-load tariffs, and legislation (House-passed Ratepayer Protection      Act) aim to assign full incremental costs to the data centers (generation, transmission, distribution upgrades, with financial assurances).      

Enforcement and exact allocation remain points of debate and state variation.

Some local/community investments by companies (water infrastructure, etc.). Federal role is mainly permitting facilitation and land access rather than direct primary funding. Companies also seek various tax breaks.
⁠Americanbanker⁠
Brookings⁠
Fox News

Environmental and Resource Impacts

Impacts are significant and localized, with right-leaning sources often noting community concerns while stressing efficiency gains, proper siting, cost internalization, and the economic/AI stakes (rather than climate-focused framing alone):

Water resources: 
Direct cooling use is substantial (billions of gallons industry-wide; projections of growth without efficiency measures). Indirect use via power plants can be larger.      
Examples of high local consumption, unbilled use, or pressure drops appear in coverage (Georgia, etc.). 

Efficiency is improving (some air-cooled or      advanced systems; company sustainability reports claim better water-use effectiveness). Strain is acute in arid regions; Texas and others have pushed reporting and compliance. Companies sometimes fund local water projects. 
Commerce Secretary Lutnick has called some water claims exaggerated or adversarial propaganda, though data show real consumption.
⁠WSJ⁠
Breitbart
⁠Breitbart

Air quality: 
Backup diesel generators, associated natural-gas plants, and operations can contribute emissions and      local pollution. Noise from cooling is a frequent complaint. Some projects include on-site generation.

Land fertility and green areas: 
Large footprints (hundreds of acres to thousands for campuses, with buffers) convert farmland, forests, or open land. Opposition is common on agricultural sites. 
Proposals for federal land use have raised concerns      about reduced review. These reduce local access to green/open space and can affect soil/agriculture in surrounding areas.

Overall environment: 
Energy intensity is high (often met by gas or mixed sources; renewables + batteries also used but with cost and reliability trade-offs). Climate pledges of the companies are complicated by the scale of new demand. Local spills, wastewater issues, and heat have occurred. Sources like RealClearEnergy and WSJ emphasize that with full cost recovery by the facilities, grid upgrades, and community standards, the projects can proceed without shifting burdens, while blanket restrictions risk economic and competitive costs. 

Local and state rules (water reporting, noise, full cost recovery, siting limits) are the main response mechanisms.⁠
Foreignpolicy⁠
Realclearenergy

In short, right-leaning reporting frames the boom as a private, market-driven AI infrastructure race that the administration is accelerating for competitiveness, with the key policy fights centered on ensuring data centers fully fund their power and resource needs so residents are not left with higher bills or depleted local resources. Outcomes vary sharply by state and locality.

What is the impact on rural area

GROK says:

Rural areas are the primary target for new data centers, creating sharp trade-offs between economic opportunity and pressure on farmland, water, electricity, and community character.

Roughly two-thirds of planned U.S. data centers are slated for rural locations (versus most existing ones in urban areas), drawn by cheaper contiguous land, available transmission, and relatively fewer neighbors or permitting hurdles. Right-leaning coverage (especially WSJ and Fox News) highlights both the potential gains for struggling rural economies and the strong local resistance, particularly from farmers.⁠
WSJ

Land, Farmland, and Agriculture

Data centers permanently convert agricultural land. Examples include Meta acquiring about 2,700 acres of rice fields in rural Louisiana for a massive campus, and utility or developer purchases of grazing land in Montana. Family farms in places like Kentucky have rejected multimillion-dollar offers (one mother-daughter pair turned down roughly $26 million for hundreds of acres held for generations) specifically to keep land in agriculture rather than see it become a hyperscale site. Farmers and ranchers warn of lost productive acreage, upward pressure on land prices that makes it harder for new or expanding operators to buy, and competition for water already heavily used for irrigation. Texas agricultural officials and rural residents have pushed back on projects moving into farm and ranch country, citing risks to the food supply and rural character. Once converted, sites rarely return to farming.
⁠WSJ⁠
WSJ

Economic and Fiscal Impacts

Benefits can be substantial where projects succeed and costs are properly managed:

Construction and jobs: 
Multi-year construction employment (hundreds to thousands of workers in skilled trades) plus ongoing roles in operations, maintenance, and security. 

Permanent staffing is lower than construction peaks but often higher-paying than local averages (examples project averages well above regional medians).

Tax revenue: 
Data centers can dominate local tax bases with relatively small land footprints. In Quincy,      Washington—a longstanding farming town that hosted Microsoft and others for ~20 years—data centers have paid a large majority of local taxes.      
Revenue funded a new high school, hospital, library, public safety  facilities, and other infrastructure while supporting population growth and cutting the poverty rate roughly in half. Property tax burdens on      residents dropped relative to what they would have been. Loudoun County, Virginia (a major hub, more exurban), has seen data centers supply around 45% of local tax revenue and generate large estimated savings for homeowners. 
Proposals such as “data center dividends” (sharing a portion of property-tax revenue directly with local households) and state-level plans (e.g., West Virginia dedicating a large share of project revenue to      income-tax reduction) aim to spread benefits more broadly in rural counties.
⁠Fox News
⁠Fox News⁠
Fox News

Caveats noted in coverage include relatively modest permanent headcounts compared with the scale of investment or incentives, and the risk that temporary construction gains do not fully translate into lasting local employment. Some rural areas view the projects as a potential economic lifeline after declines in farming or manufacturing jobs.

Electricity, Water, and Resource Strain

Rural grids and water systems face concentrated demand. A single large campus can consume power comparable to a small city, potentially driving rate increases for residents and farms (where electricity is essential for irrigation, drying, storage, and processing) unless data centers fully cover incremental generation, transmission, and distribution costs. 
This is a central concern in right-leaning reporting and has prompted state-level rules (e.g., in Texas and elsewhere) requiring large loads to pay their own way. Water use for cooling competes with agricultural needs; volumes can be high, though efficiency measures (closed-loop systems, industrial water reuse) can reduce potable draw. Quincy partnered on reuse infrastructure that significantly cut reliance on local groundwater. Dry or irrigation-dependent rural regions are especially sensitive.
⁠WSJ⁠
WSJ

Community and Quality-of-Life Effects

Opposition is often intense in rural and farming communities, even in conservative areas. Residents cite noise from cooling equipment, loss of open or agricultural land, changes to the local character, potential utility bill impacts, and limited permanent jobs relative to the footprint. Polling shows substantial rural resistance to nearby projects (though support can be higher for remote sites). Success stories like Quincy are cited by companies and some officials as models of long-term integration when tax revenue is retained locally, energy rates are protected, and water infrastructure is upgraded. Many other rural localities have imposed moratoriums, rejected rezonings, or delayed projects amid public pushback.
⁠WSJ
⁠Fox News

In right-leaning accounts, the rural impact hinges on execution: full cost allocation so residential and farm ratepayers are not subsidizing the centers, retention of tax benefits in the community, careful siting that limits prime farmland loss, and measurable local gains in jobs and infrastructure. Where those conditions hold, some rural towns have seen clear fiscal and economic upside; where they do not, resistance and resource conflicts dominate. Outcomes vary widely by state, utility rules, and local decisions.

How do rural tax revenues compare to urban ones?

GROK says:

Data centers often deliver a larger proportional boost to tax revenue in rural areas than in urban ones, even if absolute dollar amounts are smaller. A single large project (or campus) can represent a transformative share of a small rural county’s budget, while the same facility is a more modest addition to a diversified urban tax base.

Proportional vs. Absolute Impact

Rural and small-town examples: 
In Quincy, Washington (a farming town of roughly 8,000 people that has hosted Microsoft and other      data centers for about 20 years), the facilities pay a very large share of local property taxes—reports put the figure in the range of 57–65% in some measures. This has funded a new high school, hospital, public safety facilities, and other infrastructure, supported population growth, and cut the poverty rate roughly in half. Residents have faced substantially lower      relative property tax burdens than they otherwise would have.⁠
Seattlered

Established (more exurban) hubs:      
Loudoun County, Virginia—the densest data center concentration in the U.S.—generates roughly 40–45% of its total local tax revenue from data centers (on the order of $1.2–1.3 billion annually in recent budgets).      That has supported repeated cuts in residential property tax rates (around 30% over a decade in some accounts) and estimated average homeowner      savings on the order of $5,800 per year relative to a no-data-center scenario. The absolute numbers are far larger because of the sheer volume of facilities.⁠
Fox News

A Bitcoin Policy Institute analysis (covered by Fox News) estimated that a single 1-gigawatt AI data center campus could generate enough surplus property-tax revenue in a typical rural county to support household “dividends” of roughly $4,500–$8,900 per year after funding public services—figures derived in part from Loudoun data scaled to smaller rural tax bases. Louisiana has explored related mechanisms for returning some new data center revenue to residents.
⁠Btcpolicy

Why the Difference

Rural counties start with smaller tax bases, fewer households, and less diversified commercial activity. Adding high-value taxable equipment (servers are often taxed as personal property) and real estate can therefore dominate the local revenue picture and enable lower residential rates or new spending without population growth that strains services. Urban and denser metro areas already have broader residential, commercial, and industrial bases, so the same investment is a smaller percentage of total revenue. They also tend to capture more indirect economic spillovers (suppliers, local spending, specialized labor) because of existing networks.

Right-leaning sources (Fox News, WSJ, Tax Foundation commentary) frequently highlight the property-tax relief potential—especially for homeowners—when facilities pay full freight without heavy abatements. Quincy is often cited as a positive long-running rural model. Some red states (e.g., discussions around Wyoming) view data centers as a way to expand the tax base and ease homeowner burdens.

Important Caveats

Net revenue depends heavily on negotiated incentives, abatements, or payments in lieu of taxes, which are common and can substantially reduce collections in both rural and urban settings. Permanent direct employment is usually modest relative to capital investment (dozens to a few hundred jobs), so the main local fiscal upside is tax revenue rather than payroll. Some research finds metropolitan counties capture larger broader economic gains (jobs, wages, business activity) than pure rural ones because of denser ecosystems. Federal incentives aimed at rural opportunity zones may further encourage rural siting.

In short, rural areas often see a bigger share of their budgets transformed by data centers, while mature urban/exurban clusters generate higher absolute tax dollars and more secondary economic activity. Outcomes vary sharply with local tax structure, abatement deals, and whether ratepayers are protected from related infrastructure costs.

text:
Broadcom's Boss Said AI Investors Have No Clue. Chips Have Fallen 8 Days Straight

On Monday, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan sat on a panel at a conference in Singapore and said "a lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in." He compared the AI trade to a casino, and Broadcom sells a lot of the chips going into it.

By Friday the PHLX Semiconductor Index was down 11.41% for the week, its worst since April 2025, and it had closed lower 8 sessions in a row. Broadcom itself fell 9.07%.

And here's my favorite part. During that same losing streak, somebody put about $3.8 billion into SOXL, the triple-leveraged chip fund, which Kobeissi had on pace for its biggest week of inflows on record.

The scoreboard for the week:

- S&P 500: 7,659.44, down 1.95%, worst week since June
- Nasdaq: 26,140.03, down 4.48%
- Dow: 52,002.41, up 0.67%
- Russell 2000: down 3.05%
- VIX: 19.99, highest close since July 29

The Dow finishing green while the Nasdaq lost 4.5% tells you where the money went: Coca-Cola (up 6.64%), Walmart (up 6.70%) and Procter & Gamble (up 5.37%). Consumer staples gained 5.02% in the same week tech lost 7.70%. Somebody sold Nvidia and bought toothpaste

The ones who borrowed got hit hardest

If you read just a single section, make it this one.

Nvidia lost 6.61% this week. The 8 listed neoclouds, the companies that borrow money to buy Nvidia chips and rent them out to AI labs, lost an average of 22.29%, per Portfolio Terminal's count. CoreWeave was down about 25% on the week, and its unsecured bonds due 2032 traded near a 15% yield midweek.

Wednesday did the most damage. Gartner put out a forecast that more than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be exposed to impairment by 2030, and said it expects more than 80% of neocloud providers to stop operating independently by then. CoreWeave fell 15.46% that day. Oracle fell 8.83%.

On Thursday Jensen Huang told Bloomberg that "CoreWeave's strength is improving every day," and said Nvidia doesn't need to backstop it. The stock bounced 5.94%. On Friday it fell 11.91%.

Lenders now want about 15% from a company Nvidia says is getting stronger every day, and every other company that borrowed for GPUs gets priced against that. So who else borrowed for data centers?

The thing that confused people: hot inflation, lower rates

Wednesday's CPI came in hot. Prices were up 3.7% from a year ago, a tenth above forecasts, and core was 2.6%, also a tenth above. Thursday's producer prices were worse: up 1.3% in a single month, the most since March 2022, with gasoline alone up 20.3% at the wholesale level.

2 hot inflation prints in 2 days, and the 10-year Treasury yield still closed the week at 5.098%, down from 5.244% the Friday before. It touched 5.329% right after CPI and slid from there.

The bond market worries about 2 things, inflation and a slowdown, and this week the slowdown fear won. Money running out of AI stocks needed somewhere safe to sit, and a 10-year Treasury paying over 5% was an easy place to put it. All that buying pushes bond prices up, which pushes yields down. Long Treasury funds like TLT gained 2.65% in a week when the Nasdaq lost 4.48%.

On the Fed, futures put only about a 15% chance on a hike at the Oct 27 to 28 meeting after Chair Kevin Warsh refused to give any guidance in Bangkok on Friday. Goldman's economists expect a pause in October and a "second and final hike in December."

Why your mortgage rate didn't move

Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed was 7.40% on Thursday, unchanged from last week and still the highest in nearly 3 years. A year ago it was 6.27%. The 15-year eased to 6.71%.

The lower 10-year didn't show up because Freddie's survey is built from applications sent in Monday through Wednesday, and the 10-year did most of its falling Thursday. If it stays near 5.1%, next Thursday's number is the one to watch, and if you're shopping it's worth getting a fresh quote Monday.

On the other side of the table, Redfin counted 62.6% more sellers than buyers in September, the widest gap since 2013. Redfin's own economist called it a buyer's market "born out of caution, not strength." There are plenty of houses and not many people who can make the payment at 7.4%.

The household bills

Social Security announced a 3.6% cost-of-living raise for 2027 the same morning CPI came in at 3.7%, so retirees get a raise a tenth below inflation.

Real hourly pay fell 0.5% in September alone, per the BLS, and it's down 0.7% from a year ago. A Goldman Sachs survey had the share of workers increasing their retirement savings falling to 39% from 55%.

Retail sales rose 0.8%, but only 0.2% without gas stations. A lot of that spending was people paying more at the pump.

Steel hit $1,255 a ton, up 52% in a year and the highest since May 2022, with tariffs keeping imports out. That shows up later in the price of houses, cars and washing machines.

And then there's the iPhone Duo. Apple's first foldable costs $1,999, and within about half an hour of preorders opening Friday, Apple's own store was showing Jan 25 delivery for every color and storage size, while eBay listings asked up to about $5,000.

The banks

JPMorgan earned $5.57 a share, or $5.75 without a one-time item, under the $5.93 FactSet consensus, and slipped 0.86%. Bank of America fell about 4.7% on Wednesday after a $1.2 billion anti-money-laundering settlement and bond trading revenue down 17%. Wells Fargo's provisions for bad loans jumped 51%.

The one I'd actually remember is Schwab. Margin loans, money customers borrow against their stocks, jumped 14% in the 3 months through September to $187.9 billion, and they're up 93% from a year ago. About $60.7 billion of that is tied to long/short strategies, but that's still a lot of borrowed money sitting in accounts heading into a week when chips fell 11%

Washington

The government closed its books on fiscal 2026 this week. The deficit was $1.99 trillion, the third biggest on record behind 2020 and 2021. Net interest on the debt was $1.05 trillion, up from $970 billion. That's about 19.5 cents of every dollar the government collected going to interest. With the 10-year still above 5%, that bill keeps growing as older, cheaper debt rolls over at today's rates.

On Iran, President Trump told Newsmax he wouldn't use nuclear weapons or send ground troops, but said the US may have to strike Pickaxe Mountain, an underground site near Natanz. That mostly repeated what he'd already said, including last week's line that the US won't attack Iran before the midterms. The energy ceasefire he tried to broker between Russia and Ukraine came apart within days, and Zelenskyy said Kyiv would go back to hitting Russian refineries.

Oil, briefly

November WTI closed Friday at $101.41, up 10.41% on the week, and December Brent touched $110 before closing at $109.86, the highest Brent close since May. CNBC counted at least 9 ships attacked near Hormuz from last Sunday through Friday. The IEA is pushing out the last 100 million barrels of March's emergency release, diesel first, and the US offered up to 17 million SPR barrels as an exchange that refiners pay back with extra barrels later

Around the world

- Indonesia: the main index fell 11.57% Friday, its worst day since January 1998, after MSCI proposed moving the country from emerging market to standalone status. UBS estimates about $4 billion of forced passive selling if it happens
- South Korea: the KOSPI fell 5.46% Tuesday and SK Hynix 10.09% on heavy foreign selling and reports that Chinese memory maker CXMT plans a more compact server DRAM chip by year-end
- Central banks: Warsh called it "a synchronous tightening" around the world and said there are "no free riders."

Crypto

Bitcoin dipped below $80,000 early Friday, to about $79,800, before getting back to around $81,000. It's down about 2% on the week and about 7% on the year. Gold slipped about 0.6%.

For a week when people were scared of tech, bitcoin traded like tech

Trade ideas I'm chewing on

These are ideas I'm watching, not recommendations. Do your own homework

1. Boring stuff over chips, for now
- Thesis: staples, health care and dividend payers took the money tech gave up. SCHD gained 3.96% while QQQ lost 5.52%. Meta and Tesla report Wednesday, and if either sounds cautious on AI spending, that rotation has more room.
- What proves it wrong: the chip index snapping its losing streak and getting back most of the 11% within 2 weeks
- Risk: the SOXL crowd is right. Oversold chip stocks can rip 10% in days, and staples look silly fast when that happens

2. Long Treasuries as the tech hedge
- Thesis: this week bonds did their job. Yields fell even on hot inflation, because scared money wants a safe 5%. If the AI selloff keeps going, that bid keeps going.
- What proves it wrong: the 10-year back above Wednesday's 5.329% high, which would mean inflation fear is winning again
- Risk: Warsh doesn't do forward guidance, so a surprise hike Oct 28 isn't impossible, and long bonds drop hard when that happens

3. Watch the bonds of the borrowers
- Thesis: CoreWeave's 2032 bonds near 15% are the warning light for every company that borrowed to buy GPUs.
- What proves it wrong: those yields falling back toward the 13% range they traded at earlier this month, with Meta keeping its spending plans intact Wednesday
- Risk: Nvidia and the big labs have every reason to keep their customers alive. A new funding deal could squeeze anyone betting against them

Not financial advice

Next week

- Fed blackout: officials went quiet Saturday and stay quiet through Oct 29 ahead of the Oct 27 to 28 meeting
- Tue Oct 20: housing starts and permits. Earnings from GM, GE Aerospace, 3M and RTX before the open, then Netflix, Capital One and United after the close
- Wed Oct 21: Tesla, Meta, IBM, Lam Research and Texas Instruments after the close. Meta's spending plans are the AI trade's whole week
- Thu Oct 22: jobless claims and leading indicators. Procter & Gamble, American Airlines and Lockheed Martin report
- Fri Oct 23: flash PMIs and final UMich sentiment, including inflation expectations. American Express and SLB report
- Further out: Brazil's runoff Oct 25, the Fed Oct 28, and the Nov 3 midterms

Meta on Wednesday is the one I'd circle. If they keep spending, the chip crowd probably gets its bounce, and if they pull back, SOXL holders are in for another rough week

Thanks for reading all the way down here. Hope everyone has a great Sunday, and maybe check what's in your 401(k) before Wednesday

October 17, 2026

Global Macro & Central Bank Outlook: Tech Sell-Off Drags S&P 500 and Nasdaq Lower
U.S. equity benchmarks closed out Friday under heavy selling pressure, as a deepening rout in big tech and semiconductor heavyweights dragged indexes down to cap off a painful trading week. The S&P 500 fell 1.95% to close at 7,659.44. The Nasdaq led the downside, plunging 4.48% across the week to finish at 26,140.03 as persistent concerns over artificial intelligence capital expenditures hit chipmakers like Micron and Intel. The Dow Jones Industrial Average showed relative resilience, gaining 0.67% on the week to settle at 52,002.41, bolstered by defensive rotation into consumer staples and healthcare. Fixed-income yields eased modestly into the close, with the 10-Year Treasury yield slipping 15 basis points to 5.09% as safe-haven duration demand absorbed the market shock.

Geopolitical & Energy Security: WTI Crude Closes at $99.04 on Hormuz Transit Bottlenecks
Energy markets erupted to the upside into Friday's close as physical supply anxieties and maritime friction across the Persian Gulf reached a boiling point. November West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil futures (/CL) surged over 7.8% on the week to settle at $99.04 per barrel, breaking back toward $100 as maritime tracking confirmed Strait of Hormuz commercial crude transit remains severely restricted. International benchmark Brent crude spiked over 4.5% to settle near $109.86 per barrel. In precious metals, Comex December gold futures (/GC) settled around $4,188.90 per ounce as safe-haven demand re-accelerated into the weekend close.

Fiscal Dominance & Economic Policy: Cool Payrolls vs Sticky Inflation Ahead of CPI
Capitol Hill policy debates and Treasury operations continue to center on domestic borrowing management and federal revenue integrity. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced he will skip upcoming international finance summits in Bangkok to remain in Washington addressing domestic fiscal priorities. Macro policy desks digested labor statistics showing nonfarm payroll growth slowing to 29,000 jobs with unemployment rising to 4.2%, easing immediate economic overheating fears. However, with consumer and producer prices running hotter than expected and recent gas price spikes keeping inflation concerns alive, market participants are heavily focused on monetary policy expectations to determine whether energy costs force another Fed rate hike before year end.

Domestic Security & Political Landscape: Reconciliation 3.0 Border Allocations & Midterm Maps
Bipartisan friction remains high on Capitol Hill as Senate and House leadership work to enforce sweeping security frameworks codified under Reconciliation 3.0 legislative packages. The enacted provisions secure permanent funding streams for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection operational infrastructure. Concurrently, with midterm elections approaching, domestic political battles are intensifying as federal court decisions regarding state congressional redistricting maps reshape regional campaign strategies and state committees finalize grassroots operations ahead of upcoming legislative sessions.

CME Agricultural Complex: Row Crops Close Mixed; Cattle Rally into Weekend
Futures across the CME Group complex delivered active two-way trading into Friday's close. In row crops, benchmark December Corn (/ZCZ26) fell to settle at $4.73 per bushel, tumbling under seasonal Midwest harvest hedge pressure. November Soybeans (/ZSX26) settled slightly lower at $12.60 per bushel. In the livestock pits, cattle futures gained ground into the weekend; active December Live Cattle (/LEZ26) settled near $225.15 per cwt, supported by firming northern dressed cash sales at $350–$355. November Feeder Cattle (/GFX26) held a steady baseline near $341.90 per cwt.

Corporate & Energy Infrastructure: Grid Expansion Meets AI Demands; Tech Capex Worries Mounting
Single-stock news flows were dominated by Big Tech capital expenditure anxiety and midstream energy execution. Hardware and semiconductor names faced aggressive profit-taking as institutional investors continue to question ROI timelines for enterprise AI buildouts. In energy infrastructure, midstream pipeline operators report steady cash flow profiles insulated by long-term transport contracts as utility providers expand baseline grid capacity to feed growing computing demand from artificial intelligence data centers. Concurrently, domestic critical mineral producers continue expanding processing infrastructure for heavy rare earth oxides to shield supply chains from foreign trade restrictions.

Upcoming Market Expectations (October 19 – October 23)
Investors prepare for a pivotal macro week driven by central bank speeches, regional manufacturing gauges, and corporate earnings rollouts:

Monday (October 19): Federal Reserve Regional Economic Surveys & Central Bank Commentary. Global currency and commodity desks will evaluate early Asian and European trade flows alongside Fed speaker rhetoric.

Talarico Attack HYPOCRITICAL AD
DOESN'T GIVE ALL OF THE INFORMATION TO SWAY PUBLIC PERCEPTION. 
WHILE HE PROMOTES DEFUNDING POLICE AND LETTING CRIMINALS OUT OF JAIL.

Texas Democratic U.S. Senate nominee James Talarico released a political advertisement attacking Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton over a plea deal in a child sex abuse case.

The Ad's Claims

• Target: Attorney General Ken Paxton.
• Core Subject: The ad focuses on Waco attorney Adam Hoffman, who was accused of repeatedly sexually abusing a young boy under the age of 10.
• The Deal: The ad criticizes Paxton's office for offering a plea agreement that let Hoffman plead guilty to misdemeanors and face a minimal jail sentence rather than life in prison. Talarico labels it an "Epstein-style sweetheart deal for a well-connected child predator".

Context and Response

• Case Background: The case was handled by Paxton’s office after the local district attorney recused himself. The initial trial ended in a hung jury (7–5 split), and prosecutors from Paxton's office stated they offered the plea because the young victim did not want to endure testifying in a second trial.
• Jail Time: While the office initially discussed a very short sentence, Hoffman ultimately served around 30 days (with disputes over whether it was 30 or 60 days depending on the final judge's sign-off), and the plea documents did not classify the crime in a way that required him to register as a sex offender under certain terms.
• Family's Reaction: The family of the victim publicly stated they felt used for political purposes by the campaign attacks.
• Paxton's Defense: Paxton’s campaign and defenders pushed back, noting that the decision was driven by career prosecutors trying to protect the young victim from retraumatization, and countered by pointing out outside donor connections tied to Talarico.
