text:
Why do I refer to myself as infamous in the post? It’s not because the nipple pierced pink hair members of the Konrad Haters Club™️ over on bluesky.

Senior year at the greatest nautical college in the world, you get custom coveralls with the training ship embroidered on the back and your nickname on the front.

My nickname was “Infamous.”

Partly because I’d accumulated the most demerits in recent school history. My record was eventually broken by a kid who took TEN YEARS to graduate, which frankly feels like cheating. If you spend a decade collecting demerits at a four-year college, that’s not a record. That’s a career.

But what made me infamous wasn’t the number of demerits. It was how I escaped the consequences.

Maritime academies have a threshold of demerits beyond which you’re expelled so most of my competitors were gone before coming close.

But I found a loophole… if you successfully appeal, convince someone to “lose” the triplicate paperwork, obtain a pardon from the Admiral, or perform some sufficiently noble act to offset your crimes, those demerits no longer count toward expulsion.

By the end of freshman year, I’d accumulated enough demerits to qualify for a dishonorable discharge from several third world navies, but through begging, borrowing, stealing, creative paperwork management, and occasional acts of conspicuous virtue, I’d somehow remained enrolled.

My other survival strategy was avoiding Commander Kenny, the school’s deputy commandant, at all cost.

Kenny was a grizzled Vietnam-era Army NCO who had somehow gotten himself commissioned as an O-5 in the Merchant Marine, a miracle I never dared investigate. He had the disposition of an inebriated & rabid German shepherd.

This worked until the end of freshman year, when everyone boarded our 565-foot training ship for the summer voyage to Europe.

It’s relatively easy to avoid someone on a college campus. It’s considerably harder aboard a ship, where the only reliable escape routes involve swimming.

Shortly after getting underway, the regiment assembled in a massive cargo hold for uniform inspection. The captain gave a speech. The commandant gave another. Then Kenny stepped forward.

“I only have one question,” he announced.

“Where is the INFAMOUS Cadet Konrad, AND HOW THE HELL HAS HE MANAGED TO AVOID DETENTION?”

Every head turned toward me.

“THE CRACKDOWN BEGINS NOW, KONRAD.”

He made my summer a living hell.

If something needed scraping, chipping, painting, cleaning, or extracting from a compartment that smelled like Satan’s septic tank after a swingers convention hosted by the Golden Corral, Kenny made certain I was the first to be voluntold.

But he’d overlooked one important detail.

I loved being at sea.

I loved ships, hard work, foreign ports, and practically everything about the profession. So while he was attempting to break my spirit through manual labor, I was mostly having a wonderful time.

I also may or may not have discovered that certain particularly unpleasant jobs required specialized tools, and that those tools had a mysterious tendency to relocate themselves to Davy Jones’ locker.

An old salt aboard once offered me some wisdom:

“Shit rolls downhill, kid. But ever since they invented the block and tackle, we’ve been able to haul it right back up.”

Words to live by.

Eventually, Kenny and I reached a truce, partly because he couldn’t figure out how to punish someone who genuinely enjoyed working aboard ship.

And partly because even the most disciplined ship occasionally needs something unusual accomplished in a foreign port.

Special provisions. Impossible favors. Bureaucratic obstacles that need to disappear.

And who better for the captain to call than the cadet with a demonstrated talent for accomplishing things without leaving behind a paper trail?

Which brings me back to the coveralls. 1/2

This past Monday I was out on the trails at Guana in NE Florida. While on the orange trail I encountered another hiker at a cross point and offered him water since he was not carrying any. We ended up heading the same direction so we struck up some small talk about where we were from and how long we had been in the area, and during the conversation learned we had both been at the Phish concert in Jacksonville the Friday before. I also learned he had never seen an alligator in the wild, so I showed him one of my observation spots and he got to see a baby that was out. We went our separate ways, but about 30 minutes later, crossed paths again and chatted a little more. We started talking about Goose and he mentioned he was trying to go to their shows in Nashville next month. I’m going to those shows myself and am trying to connect with this hiking trail stranger again. He seemed like a really cool, kind, jam band dude, so I want to try and find him and connect again- like bromance serendipity, I guess? 🤣

His name was either Brayden or Bryson. I’m horrible with names. So, if you’re out there and see this… let’s connect.

These are distinct from the larger number of states that have passed laws requiring parental notification or clarifying that not affirming a gender identity is not abuse.
Here are the most prominent examples:
Washington: SB 5599 (2023, signed by Gov. Jay Inslee)
This law changes notification rules for licensed shelters, host homes, and programs serving runaway or homeless youth. If a minor is seeking or receiving “gender-affirming treatment” (or reproductive health care), the facility can notify the state Department of Children, Youth & Families instead of the parents. The state is then supposed to offer family reunification services. 
Critics (including lawsuits and amicus briefs from other states) argue it allows children to be sheltered without parental knowledge or involvement when they are seeking gender-related medical interventions. Supporters say it protects runaway youth from potential abuse or neglect and does not change medical consent laws or authorize the state to permanently remove children. The law has faced legal challenges that reached higher courts.
California: AB 1955 / SAFETY Act (2024, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom)
This law prohibits school districts from requiring employees or contractors to disclose a student’s sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression to anyone (including parents) without the student’s consent. It also bars districts from enforcing “forced outing” policies. 
It was passed in response to several local school districts that had adopted policies requiring parental notification if a student requested different names, pronouns, or use of opposite-sex facilities. Critics say it allows schools to facilitate social transitions without parents’ knowledge. California officials have stated it does not prohibit staff from disclosing information if they choose to, and parents retain access to official education records under FERPA. The law has been the subject of ongoing federal and state court challenges.
Colorado: Kelly Loving Act (HB 25-1312, 2025)
As originally introduced, this bill would have required courts in custody cases to treat “deadnaming,” “misgendering,” or threats related to gender-affirming care as forms of “coercive control.” That would have been a mandatory factor when determining parenting time and the best interests of the child. 
Those specific custody provisions were stripped out before the bill passed and was signed into law. A similar provision in a 2026 bill was also removed. The final version of the Kelly Loving Act focuses on other anti-discrimination measures.
Other Related Cases and Context
There are documented cases (not always tied to a single new statute) of child protective services investigations or temporary removals in states including California, Oregon, Indiana, Maryland, and Virginia involving parents who refused to use preferred names/pronouns or consent to social or medical transition. Outcomes vary: some parents were later cleared, some cases involved co-occurring mental health or medical issues (e.g., eating disorders), and some parents allege non-affirmation was treated as a key factor. In 2026, the federal Administration for Children and Families issued guidance reminding states that declining to affirm a child’s gender identity is not, by itself, abuse under federal child welfare law.
In contrast, states such as Indiana, Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina, Tennessee, West Virginia, Alabama, and others have enacted laws requiring schools to notify parents of requests for name/pronoun changes or social transition. Several states (including Texas, North Carolina, and Indiana) have also clarified that raising a child consistent with biological sex does not constitute abuse.

text:
When a Service Dog Retires, Honoring a Working Life
Sunday, Oct 18, 2026

Every working dog eventually hangs up the harness. Retirement is one of the hardest and most loving decisions a service dog team makes, and there is no single right age.

Guide Dogs for the Blind says retirement comes at different times in life. Dogs with heavier workloads, busier lifestyles or health concerns may retire younger, while others work into their senior years. A dog may lose the usual pep in its step or its enthusiasm for the work, and the handler, who knows the dog best, is often the first to notice the work losing its normal sharpness.

Canadian Guide Dogs for the Blind retires its guides at a maximum age of eleven, and earlier if a dog develops health issues, slows down or shows guiding behavior that could become a safety issue. Guide Dogs, the UK sight loss charity, starts discussing retirement when a dog is around eight years old, though the dog may keep working a few more years. It recommends vet checkups every six months until age nine, then every three months.

Where does a retired dog go? Many stay home as a beloved pet. Guide Dogs for the Blind gives handlers who have worked with their dog for twelve months or longer the first option to keep their guide or place the dog with a trusted family member or friend. Otherwise it offers the dog to its puppy raisers, then finds another loving home.

Feelings of grief and loss are normal when a partnership ends, Guide Dogs notes, and talking with friends, family or fellow handlers can help. Here at home, our own Odin is 8 1/2 and went almost blind this past year, adapting with his nose and ears. Every dog ages on its own timeline, and every one of them has earned a soft landing.

Watch Dogs of Service from Iowa PBS on YouTube

Sources: Guide Dogs for the Blind client guidance on retirement, Canadian Guide Dogs for the Blind FAQ via @CDNGuideDogs, Guide Dogs UK retirement guidance via @guidedogs, photos via Wikimedia Commons by DASGAK zzo Hoamiie, CC0, Whispyhistory, CC0, and Atlas815, CC BY SA 4.0.

text:
The Nature of Sin: A Biblical, Lexical, and Confessional Analysis

Jack Kettler

Abstract

This paper offers a concise theological examination of the nature of sin according to Scripture and the Reformed confessional tradition. Sin is defined as any want of conformity to or active transgression of the moral law of God, encompassing both sins of commission and sins of omission. The study draws on key biblical texts, the Westminster Shorter Catechism, lexical analysis of the principal New Testament terms for sin, and Charles Hodge’s systematic exposition. It further situates the doctrine of sin in relation to original sin, total depravity, and the Fall, before concluding with the biblical and confessional resolution of human sin in the person and work of Christ.

Keywords: sin, law of God, commission, omission, original sin, total depravity, imputation, Reformed theology

1. Introduction

The doctrine of sin holds a foundational place in Christian theology, especially in the Reformed tradition. A precise understanding of sin is indispensable to a coherent account of the human condition, the necessity of redemption, and the work of Christ. This paper examines the nature of sin by integrating biblical testimony, confessional standards, lexical evidence, and classical systematic theology. The aim is to set forth a clear, historically grounded definition of sin and to show how it is resolved through the satisfaction and imputation accomplished by Jesus Christ.

2. Definition of Sin

“Sin may be defined as any lack of conformity, whether active or passive, to the moral law of God. This deficiency may appear in an act, a thought, or an inward disposition or state

Two complementary aspects are customarily distinguished. A sin of “commission” consists in the deliberate transgression of the revealed will of God—the explicit breaking of divine law. A sin of “omission” consists in the ethical failure to perform that which one is able and obliged to perform—the absence of conformity to what the law requires. In an active sense, the doing of what God forbids constitutes a sin of commission. In a negative sense, the failure to do what God commands constitutes a sin of omission.

Illustrative sins of commission include blasphemy, fornication, adultery, homosexuality, lying, drunkenness, murder, and slander. Illustrative sins of omission include remaining silent in the face of falsehood, withholding the truth, refusing to do good to those who require it when one has the power to assist, leaving necessary duties unfinished until opportunity has passed, and remaining silent in the face of evil.” (Erickson 578).

3. Biblical Foundations

Scripture confirms these definitions:

“Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law” (1 John 3:4).

This text from 1 John addresses the sin of commission.

“Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin” (James 4:17).

This text from James addresses the sin of omission.

Additional passages establish the universality of sin and the necessity of repentance and union with Christ:

·         “I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish” (Luke 13:3).

·         “My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1).

·         “And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men everywhere to repent” (Acts 17:30).

·         “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Galatians 6:7).

·         “All unrighteousness is sin: and there is a sin not unto death” (1 John 5:17).

·         “Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death” (James 1:15).

4. Confessional Definition

The Westminster Shorter Catechism (Question 14) supplies a precise formulation:

Q. What is sin?

A. Sin is any want of conformity unto, or transgression of, the law of God.

The Catechism’s proof texts are 1 John 3:4, James 4:17, and Romans 3:23 (“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God”).

5. Lexical Analysis of the New Testament Vocabulary

“W. E. Vine’s “Expository Dictionary of New Testament Words” offers a detailed treatment of the principal terms for sin. The noun “hamartia” (literally “a missing of the mark”) is the most comprehensive term for moral obliquity. It is employed (a) of sin as a principle or source of action (e.g., Rom. 3:9; 5:12, 13, 20; 6:1–2; 7:7–13); (b) of sin as a governing power personified (e.g., Rom. 5:21; 6:12, 14; 7:11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 25; 8:2); (c) as a generic term sometimes inclusive of concrete wrongdoing (e.g., John 8:21, 34, 46; 9:41; 15:22, 24; 1 John 1:7–8; 3:4, 8–9); and (d) of a specific sinful deed (e.g., Matt. 12:31; Acts 7:60; Jas. 1:15; 2:9; 4:17; 5:15, 20; 1 John 5:16).

The related noun “hamartēma” denotes an act of disobedience to divine law (e.g., Mark 3:28; Rom. 3:25; 1 Cor. 6:18). The verb “hamartanō” (“to miss the mark”) is used of sinning against God, Christ, man, one’s own body, or earthly masters (e.g., Matt. 27:4; Luke 15:18, 21; John 5:14; 8:11; Rom. 2:12; 3:23; 5:12; 6:15; 1 Cor. 6:18; 7:28; 1 John 1:10; 2:1; 3:6, 8–9). Christ is uniformly predicated as without sin in every respect (2 Cor. 5:21; 1 John 3:5; John 14:30; John 8:46; Heb. 4:15; 1 Pet. 2:22) (Vine 1045–1047).”

6. The Protestant Doctrine of Sin (Charles Hodge)

“Charles Hodge summarizes the consensus of the Protestant churches at the time of the Reformation. Founding their doctrine upon moral and religious consciousness and upon the Word of God, they defined sin as the transgression of, or want of conformity to, the divine law. Melanchthon, Gerhard, Baier, and Vitringa all employ formulations that identify sin as “anomia”—a discrepancy from, or non-congruence with, the law of God that obliges the sinner to punishment under the order of divine justice.

Hodge extracts five propositions from these definitions: (1) sin is a specific evil, differing from all other forms of evil; (2) sin stands in necessary relation to law, so that where there is no law there can be no sin; (3) the law in view is the law of God, not merely the law of reason, conscience, or expediency; (4) sin consists essentially in the want of conformity of a rational creature to the nature or law of God; and (5) sin includes both guilt and moral pollution.

Consciousness itself discloses that sin is a specific evil known immediately by moral beings. It further discloses that sin is related to law: the word “ought” implies obligation under authority. The law that binds the conscience is that which has been revealed in the constitution of human nature, the Decalogue, the Mosaic institutions, and the whole of Scripture. Sin is neither a mere limitation of being, nor a subjective state without character before God, nor merely something unwise or inexpedient; it possesses a distinct character that includes both guilt and pollution.” (Hodge, Vol. 2, 180–182).

7. Related Doctrinal Categories

·         “Original sin” denotes the sinful state and condition into which all human beings are born, comprising both imputed guilt (the guilt of Adam’s first sin reckoned to their account) and inherited corruption (a disposition toward sin).

·         “Total depravity” affirms that the inherent corruption of humankind “extends to every part of our nature, to all the faculties and powers of both soul and body; and that there is no spiritual good, that is, good in relation to God, in the sinner at all, but only perversion.”

·         The “Fall of man” refers to the disobedience of Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, whereby they transgressed the divine prohibition against eating of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, resulting in God’s curse upon them and all their posterity.

8. The Resolution of Sin in Christ

The Heidelberg Catechism (Question and Answer 56) articulates the believer’s confession concerning the forgiveness of sins:

·         Q. What believest thou concerning “the forgiveness of sins”?

·         A. That God, for the sake of Christ’s satisfaction, will no more remember my sins, neither my corrupt nature, against which I have to struggle all my life long; but will graciously impute to me the righteousness of Christ, that I may never be condemned before the tribunal of God.

The apostle Paul writes:

“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Matthew Poole comments:

“Christ knew no sin, as he was guilty of no sin… but God made him to be sin for us. He was numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12). Our sins were reckoned to him… He was made a sacrifice for our sins, a sin offering… That we might be made the righteousness of God in him; that so his righteousness might be imputed to us… As Christ was not made sin by any sin inherent in him, so neither are we made righteous by any righteousness inherent in us, but by the righteousness of Christ imputed to us” (Poole 616).

9. Conclusion

Sin is any want of conformity to, or transgression of, the law of God—whether by commission or omission, whether as principle, power, or particular act. Scripture, confessional standards, lexical data, and classical Reformed theology converge upon this definition. The universal guilt and corruption of humanity find their sole remedy in the substitutionary work of Christ, who was made sin for us that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.

Notes

1.      Millard Erickson, “Christian Theology” (Grand Rapids, MI: Baker), 578.

2.      W. E. Vine, “An Expository Dictionary of New Testament Words” (Iowa Falls, IA: Riverside Book and Bible House), 1045–1047.

3.      Charles Hodge, “Systematic Theology”, vol. 2 (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans), 180–182.

4.      Matthew Poole, “Matthew Poole’s Commentary on the Holy Bible”, vol. 3 (Peabody, MA: Hendrickson, 1985), 616.

Further Resources

·         Herman Bavinck, “The Origin of Sin,” https://t.co/5oytCJuR6g.

·         J. C. Ryle, “A True Understanding of Sin,” https://t.co/5oytCJuR6g.

·         Rebecca Writes, “Theological Terms in A–Z,” https://t.co/WYdiMx76FD.

Selected Quotations

·         “Here is a beautiful antithesis. In ourselves we are scattered, in Christ we are gathered together… Our sins overwhelm us, but they are laid on Christ by whom we are unburdened.” — John Calvin, “Sermons on Isaiah’s Prophecy of the Death and Passion of Christ”, 66–67.

·         “No one knows the one-hundredth part of the sin that clings to his soul.” — John Calvin.

·         “Sin consists in doing, saying, thinking, or imagining anything that is not in perfect conformity with the mind and law of God.” — J. C. Ryle, “Holiness”, 2.

·         “Sin is a disease which pervades and runs through every part of our moral constitution and every faculty of our minds.” — J. C. Ryle, “Holiness”, 3.

·         “Any sin is more or less heinous depending upon the honor and majesty of the one whom we had offended. Since God is of infinite honor, infinite majesty, and infinite holiness, the slightest sin is of infinite consequence.” — Jonathan Edwards.

Declaration

“For transparency, I note that I used Grok, an AI tool developed by xAI, and Grammarly AI for editorial assistance in drafting, organizing, and refining the manuscript’s clarity and grammar, as indicated in the article’s attribution. All theological arguments, exegesis, and interpretations are my own, and I take full responsibility for the content.” –  Jack Kettler

text:
Tanner McKee has a Super Bowl ring and two career starts.

Both of those starts came in the final game of a season, when nothing was on the line.

Today Jalen Hurts has a blood clot in his calf, so McKee starts for the Eagles against the Panthers.

It is the first start of his life that actually matters.

Here is the whole thing.

McKee grew up in Corona, California, and he was a big deal. Four star quarterback. Elite 11 finalist. More than 30 scholarship offers.

Then at 16 a mole on his forehead came back positive for melanoma.

Here is the scene. A 16 year old sitting in a pre op room in a surgical gown. Purple X marks drawn on his forehead and his neck. Phone in his hand, scrolling messages from college coaches offering him scholarships.

He looked at his mom and said this.

"If they only knew."

They cut it out. No chemotherapy. No radiation.

Here is his father on that week.

"Is his football career done? Are our lives going to totally change?"

Then he signed with Stanford. And then he left.

McKee belongs to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter day Saints, and he decided when he was eight years old that he would serve a mission. So at 18, with 30 offers sitting behind him, he got on a plane to Curitiba, Brazil for 21 months.

Nick Saban told him Alabama would wait.

He packed a football. For the first ten months it basically sat there.

"I remember throwing the ball over power lines and little kids being all excited."

The kids could not figure out why the ball was not round.

He lost about 15 pounds of muscle. His weight room was makeshift weights and walking.

Somebody asked if he could play right then.

"If I had to play a game right now, it would be tough. I'd get crushed."

"I'm 100 percent missionary. I'm not too worried about how I'm going to come back as an athlete."

Then one of his mission leaders tracked down a local semi pro team called the Coritiba Crocodiles and asked if they would practice with him. The players were anywhere from 14 to 40 years old. Before anybody could start they had to shoo chickens and roosters off the field, which had no lines on it.

He spent the day teaching a receiver named Athos how to high point a football.

Here is what Athos said about him.

"I identified with him because I also used to have heart issues when I was young."

McKee enrolled at Stanford at 20. In his fourth college start he beat Oregon, the number three team in the country, in overtime.

He went in the sixth round, 188th pick.

Now the honest part. He is 1 and 1 as a starter and he has under 600 passing yards in his entire NFL career. This could be one afternoon and then back to the clipboard.

But nobody else in that building put two football years down on purpose and then went and got them back.

He learned Portuguese out there. His teammates call him the Mormon Missile.

Today he gets a start that counts.

text:
They Built the World’s Largest Vineyard. We Built Over It.

The story of Rancho Cucamonga...

Before the warehouses, vineyards stood.

Before the loading docks, harvests took place.

East of Los Angeles, an Italian immigrant helped build a wine empire most Americans have never heard of.

His name was Secondo Guasti.

Around 1900, he and his investors began transforming Cucamonga’s dry, rocky land into an enormous vineyard. His Italian Vineyard Company eventually controlled roughly 5,000 acres—an operation promoted as the world’s largest vineyard.

He built a community around it: workers’ homes, a school, a store, a firehouse, a church.

Families planted roots alongside the vines.

The wider Cucamonga district became a giant of American wine. Before World War II, vineyards covered more than 27,000 acres around Rancho Cucamonga.

Then Southern California’s expansion reached the rows.

Housing. Roads. Commercial development. Eventually, immense warehouses.

The arithmetic overwhelmed the agriculture: land could bring a family far more money as a development site than as a lifetime of grape harvests.

Imagine spending decades farming—and receiving an offer that could finally secure your children’s future.

That is how a landscape disappears. One understandable decision at a time.

But another outcome was possible.

In 1968, Napa County established an agricultural preserve, restricting subdivision and prioritizing agriculture across thousands of acres.

Cucamonga’s vineyards largely gave way to the growing metropolis.

This was a working wine country. Affordable bottles. Immigrant families. Generations of knowledge carried from distant villages into California soil.

Today, surviving vineyards and preservation efforts still defend pieces of that inheritance.

They deserve our attention before the next piece disappears.

Because a century-old vine cannot be replaced by putting a grape cluster on a shopping-center sign.

We know how to calculate land value.

We are much worse at calculating the cost of losing what grows there.

text:
Yes, it is generally legal, appropriate, and common for someone to pick up food from a food bank or pantry on behalf of a disabled person who cannot go themselves.
Legality
There is no general law against helping someone obtain food assistance this way. Food banks and pantries are private nonprofits (often distributing USDA commodities under programs like TEFAP or CSFP), and they set their own rules. Most explicitly allow proxies or authorized representatives for people who are disabled, homebound, ill, or have transportation barriers.
The Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act protects good-faith food donations and distribution by nonprofits, but that is about liability for the food itself, not about proxy pickups. Proxy arrangements are a standard, accepted operational practice.
Appropriateness
It is appropriate and often encouraged. Food banks exist to help people who need food; disability or mobility issues are among the most common reasons they create proxy policies. Doing this with the person’s clear permission respects their autonomy and dignity. Many organizations also offer home delivery or other accommodations for homebound clients when available.
How Common It Is
Very common. Numerous food banks, pantries, and federal commodity programs (such as CSFP for seniors) maintain official proxy forms specifically for disability, health concerns, or transportation limitations. Examples include state CSFP programs (California, Washington, and others), regional food banks, and local pantries that require a signed authorization, household information, and sometimes ID from the proxy.
Typical requirements include:
•A signed proxy/authorization form from the client naming the person picking up.
•Basic household details (size, sometimes ages).
•The proxy presenting ID.
•Periodic renewal of the form (often annually).
Policies vary by organization—some are flexible for one-time or emergency pickups; others want the form in advance. Always check with the specific food bank or pantry beforehand.
Practical tip: Contact the food bank, explain the disability situation, and ask about their proxy process. Many will provide the form or walk you through it. Some also coordinate deliveries or other help for people who cannot leave home.
(Note: You are in British Columbia, Canada. Canadian food banks generally operate similarly and commonly allow authorized pickups or deliveries for clients who cannot attend in person, though exact rules depend on the local organization. The principles of legality and appropriateness are the same.)
In short: With the disabled person’s authorization and following the food bank’s process, this is a normal and helpful thing to do.

text:
In 1891, Billy Sunday walked away from about $400 a month (roughly $14,000 today) to take a job that paid $83.

He was one of the fastest players in baseball, and Philadelphia had just signed him to a three-year deal. He had a new baby at home and an invalid brother to support.

But four years earlier, he had been drinking with teammates outside a Chicago saloon when a gospel band marched by. 

He followed them into the Pacific Garden Mission and walked out a Bible-believing Christian. He could not shake the feeling that he was being called to preach full time.

He told his wife, Nell. She told him that if the Lord was talking to him, he had better listen.

So, he asked for his release. When word got out, Cincinnati offered him even more money. He said no to them too and went to work for the Chicago YMCA.

He never stopped playing ball, though. He just brought it to the pulpit. Sunday sprinted across the stage, slid into imaginary bases, stood on chairs, and pounded the furniture. He preached like a man trying to beat out a throw to first.

Twenty years later he was the most famous preacher in America. Cities had to build wooden tabernacles to hold his crowds.

By some estimates he preached to 100 million people without a microphone.
